They did not become the celebrated destroyers of slavery until almost two years into the war, with the Emancipation Proclamation, issued Jan. 1, 1863. docs.lead_paragraph: In 2007, a virus called infectious salmon anemia started killing millions of farm-raised salmon in Chile and devastated Chilean aquaculture. The virus was first detected in 1984 — long before salmon farming had spread around the globe — but what made it so lethal in 2007 was overcrowding in the offshore salmon pens and the fact that salmon were being raised in the midst of their own pollution. No one knew how the virus was transmitted, but a 2008 study at the University of Bergen determined it was carried in salmon eggs exported from Norway to Chile.

docs.lead_paragraph: Mathematical folklore is rife with legends of imprisoned people who won their freedom or escaped death by solving a mathematical problem. We’ve featured a number of such problems here including the Josephus Problem, which, according to legend, allowed the 1st-century Jewish historian Flavius Josephus to save himself from death. (In our version, it was a firing game featuring Donald Trump and Ryan Seacrest.) We’ve also featured the Prisoners and Light Bulb problem and the Prisoners and the File Drawers problem, in both of which prison authorities give their detainees a mathematical problem to solve to gain their freedom. Today’s puzzle features a similar scenario. It concerns a medieval king who, in a rare fit of potential mercy, promises to free 5 of his prisoners on condition that they solve a problem. This problem is based on a submission by the prolific Numberplay contributor Ravi Kumar Meduri, from Hyderabad, India.

headline.main: Numberplay: The Keys to Freedom

It also accumulated more than 8 million total viewers, up from 6.9 million last week. “60 minutes” did its part as well for CBS, as it was once again the most-watched program of the night with 8.8 million viewers. Meanwhile, “The Bachelorette: The Men Tell All Special” won the 9 p.m. time slot for ABC in total viewers with 5.1 million but was down considerably compared with last season’s edition, which drew 8.9 million. Still, it gave ABC its best summer Sunday rating with entertainment programming in five years (the 2010 special appeared on a Monday).

docs.abstract: Darren Criss has become popular recently on the Fox series “Glee” playing a gay high school student and show choir member who exudes charisma and self-confidence.
docs.snippet: Darren Criss has become popular recently on the Fox series “Glee” playing a gay high school student and show choir member who exudes charisma and self-confidence.
docs.lead_paragraph: January is often the cruelest month for Broadway box offices, as holiday tourists head home, students go back to school and New Yorkers hibernate from the cold and snow. Last winter the lead producers of the Broadway revival of “Promises, Promises” closed the show on Jan. 2 rather than gamble money on recasting their two stars, Sean Hayes and Kristin Chenoweth, and risk a slide in ticket sales. Those same producers are now behind another Broadway revival, “How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying,” but they have opted to replace their star, Daniel Radcliffe, who finishes his run as the scheming executive J. Pierrepont Finch on New Year’s Day. Confirming rumors that have been circulating for a couple of weeks, the producers announced on Monday that Mr. Radcliffe (of “Harry Potter” fame) will be succeeded by a lesser-known actor, Darren Criss, who has become popular recently on the Fox series “Glee” playing a gay high school student and show choir member who exudes charisma and self-confidence. In casting Mr. Criss the producers are seeking to appeal to at least some of the teenagers, women and gay men who often mob Mr. Radcliffe at the stage door after performances. Mr. Criss is scheduled for only a three-week engagement, Jan. 3 through 22. In their statement announcing Mr. Criss the producers did not say if they plan to cast another actor after him, close the $8.5 million production after he departs, or try to extend his run. A spokesman for the musical said the producers had not made decisions about the future of the show after the Criss run.

headline.main: Criss to Succeed Radcliffe In ‘How to Succeed’

docs.lead_paragraph: A recent mapping expedition by scientists has shown that a zone of low oxygen in the Gulf of Mexico is above average but not as vast as many had anticipated, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said Monday. Flooding in the Midwest had stirred fears that vast amounts of farm chemicals and waste traveling down the Mississippi would create the largest “dead zone” ever. NOAA said the zone measured 6,765 square miles, which is not a record. But scientists warned that the data could be misleading because a tropical storm had roiled and mixed gulf waters. They said that levels of the chemicals that deplete oxygen were rising year to year, weakening the gulf’s resistance to pollution.

headline.main: Gulf ‘Dead Zone’ Is Smaller Than Feared

headline.main: Does Philosophy Matter?

Next year Toronto could feature an outfield of Jose Bautista, Rasmus and Travis Snider/Eric Thames, and an infield with Adam Lind, Brett Lawrie and Yunel Escobar, to go along with a power-hitting catcher in J.P. Arencibia. With Ricky Romero and Brandon Morrow developing and Brett Cecil recently building on a solid rookie year, the Jays could crash the Yanks-Sox-Rays triumvirate as early as 2012.The Indians coughed up some top pitching prospects (Drew Pomeranz and Alex White) for Ubaldo Jimenez, and it makes you wonder why the Yankees didn’t offer a similar package (including Dellin Betances and Manny Banuelos), or, if they did, why the Rockies didn’t want it. Jimenez has a good contract and is under team control through 2014, so unless Colorado suspected there was something wrong with him, this seems like a good price. It’s not entirely true that there’s no such thing as a pitching prospect, especially when you’re talking about players who blew away the high minors like Tim Lincecum and Tommy Hanson or mega-talents like David Price or Stephen Strasburg. But for the next tier down, which is how I view both the Indians’ and Yankees’ duos, the failure rate is awfully high. It’ll be interesting to see how Jimenez fares with all his starts at sea level, albeit in the American League.

docs.abstract: Avocado. Chocolate. Mushroom. Just some of the flavors featured in the fifth annual Pie Off in Portland, Ore.
docs.snippet: Avocado. Chocolate. Mushroom. Just some of the flavors featured in the fifth annual Pie Off in Portland, Ore.
docs.lead_paragraph: Trying to locate this year’s fifth annual Pie Off in Laurelhurst Park in Portland, Ore., was like a sketch from the TV show “Portlandia”: first you had to pass by what was billed (in chalk on the asphalt path) as an “organic free-range wedding,” then a free performance of Shakespeare’s “Much Ado About Nothing.” Finally, in the northeast corner of the park — marked by a bluegrass band and pennant banners made from recycled fabric, strung between the linden trees — were four tables spilling with pies. There was everything from the classic (Grandma Jane’s apple pie, berry with a lattice crust) to the quintessentially Portland (a gluten-free “Rawvocado-chocolate” — avocado, chocolate, raw macadamias, dates and shredded coconut). Hopeful eaters of all ages clustered around the tables, compostable forks and paper plates at the ready, waiting for four judges to sample all 60 pies that had been entered in one of four categories: savory, sweet non-fruit, sweet fruit and “creative.”

headline.main: All the Pie in Portland

docs.abstract: The saga of “The Meatball” and “The Worm”
docs.snippet: The saga of “The Meatball” and “The Worm”
docs.lead_paragraph: The return of the space shuttle Atlantis to the Earth’s atmosphere two weeks ago marked the close of NASA’s 30-year space shuttle program. Retirement of this popular and very visible shuttle program further strains the already diminished agency. “Space experts say the best and brightest often head for the doors when rocket lines get marked for extinction, dampening morale and creating hidden threats,” according to The Times. This is not the first time in NASA’s history when the agency faced publicity troubles. Back in 1974, after the success of the Mercury and Apollo programs, but before the initiation of the Shuttle Program, NASA was convinced by the National Endowment for the Arts to participate in its “Federal Graphics Improvement Program,” and do what many companies these days do to revive their image: undergo a redesign.Up until that point, NASA had been primarily using an insignia adapted by James Modarelli, the head of NASA’s Lewis Research Center Reports Division. This logo, created in 1959 and affectionately dubbed “The Meatball,” relied heavily on multiple visual metaphors. According to NASA’s Web site, “the sphere represents a planet, the stars represent space, the red chevron is a wing representing aeronautics (the latest design in hypersonic wings at the time the logo was developed), and then there is an orbiting spacecraft going around the wing.” Although charming in its quirkiness, the meatball proved difficult to reproduce given the printing technology available at the time and the variety of applications it would need to adorn.

headline.main: Who Made Those NASA Logos?

docs.abstract: It took the intervention of his peers to convince one business owner that if he didn’t master his finances he was going to lose his business.
docs.snippet: It took the intervention of his peers to convince one business owner that if he didn’t master his finances he was going to lose his business.
docs.lead_paragraph: In a small-business guide to accounting that we’ve just published, Darren Dahl writes about Bart Justice, who started a document-destruction business, Secure Destruction Service, in 2004. The business, based in Huntsville, Ala., grew from $70,000 in annual revenue its first year to $500,000 four years later. To finance his growth, Mr. Justice kept borrowing money from the bank, not realizing that the more he grew, the more he needed to borrow because his revenue was not covering his expenses. The loans meant he had money in his accounts — but it was borrowed money. “I knew how to print a financial statement from QuickBooks, but I couldn’t tell you what it meant,” he said. It took the intervention of business owners in a peer group Mr. Justice joined to convince him that if he didn’t master his finances he was going to lose his business.

headline.main: Do You Know Enough About Accounting?

docs.abstract: Like corpses in a bad horror movie, the women in the D.S.K. scandal pile up behind every door and under every bed. But the woman behind the man,  Anne Sinclair, has remained a somewhat shadowy figure.
docs.snippet: Like corpses in a bad horror movie, the women in the D.S.K. scandal pile up behind every door and under every bed. But the woman behind the man,  Anne Sinclair, has remained a somewhat shadowy figure.
docs.lead_paragraph: Like corpses in a bad horror movie, the women in the D.S.K. scandal pile up behind every door and under every bed. But the woman behind the man,  Anne Sinclair, has remained a somewhat shadowy figure. Vanessa Grigoriadis’s piece in New York magazine, borrowing heavily from interviews in Le Monde, Le Nouvel Observateur and the biography Madame DSK, which is currently available only in French, is filled with details of the marriage (both left spouses for each other; she prefers Paris, he their riad in Marrakesh; she broke off a friendship when her friend suggested D.S.K.’s affairs were too numerous to be forgivable even by a Frenchwoman). It also reminds us of Sinclair’s striking readiness, past and present, to stand behind and by her man, despite having a prominent career as a TV host and holding the purse strings.For those of you hankering for more of the “other woman,” it’s worth reading the account of one Marie-Victorine M. in the Daily Beast, who claims to have found D.S.K. irresistibly magnetic (their eyes met across a room and for four months they had a torrid affair), and yet who believes the account of the Sofitel maid is true. What convinced her?  “When I read the first articles in the American press containing for example the detail that he was supposed to have taken his presumed victim from behind, that encouraged me to believe this woman.”

headline.main: Cherchez la Femme

docs.abstract: A beekeeper should be thorough. I think I am, but my self-image of completeness is a wonderful façade that any master beekeeper would see through.
docs.snippet: A beekeeper should be thorough. I think I am, but my self-image of completeness is a wonderful façade that any master beekeeper would see through.
docs.lead_paragraph: It felt to me like a whole new level of bungling was needed before I met my standard of a new entry for the Beekeeper’s Journal.  Yes, I had lost both hives during an exceedingly cold snap in the preceding winter.  Yes, I had gone through the process of ordering packaged bees from Georgia and had even managed the workaround of securing two northward-trucked hives when the Georgia apiaries delayed shipment because of a devastating southern winter.  Yes, I had somehow installed the queens and hives, which involved the usual banging and subsequent pouring of nearly 3,000 bees into their new home, even though I was sure I had broken my hand earlier that day (a gangly kid on “Nature Walk” at school got tangled in my feet and dropped me to the pavement).  Yes, I watched in June as a cluster of 10,000 bees swarmed from one hive and coagulated on a tree branch sixty feet above the ground.  None of these events taken alone seemed to merit an instructive tale.  It was the swarm, however, that lay the groundwork for my recent mid-Summer bungle.

headline.main: To Split or Not to Split

docs.lead_paragraph: France approved the extradition of the former dictator Manuel Antonio Noriega to his native Panama, an official at the prime minister’s office said Wednesday. According to his lawyer, Yves Leberquier, Mr. Noriega will not be extradited before September. Last year, Mr. Noriega, left, who ruled Panama from 1983 to 1989, was sentenced by a French judge to seven years in prison for laundering $3 million in Colombian drug money through international banks and into French accounts. He had previously been jailed in Miami on charges that included cocaine trafficking. The government of Panama has requested that Mr. Noriega be extradited from France in order to serve three 20-year prison terms for human rights abuses and involvement in the disappearance of political opponents.

docs.lead_paragraph: ON screen just as on the stage the monologue lets us zero in on one character’s psychology and worldview. docs.abstract: The folk-rock group Dawes are honored – and amused – to be credited with reviving the Laurel Canyon sound.
docs.snippet: The folk-rock group Dawes are honored – and amused – to be credited with reviving the Laurel Canyon sound.
docs.lead_paragraph: Since their debut record, “North Hills,” came out two years ago, the Los Angeles-based folk-rock band Dawes has been eliciting breathless comparisons to some pretty illustrious names — Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, the Eagles, the Band. Partly it has to do with their origin myth: they recorded the album at the renowned producer Jonathan Wilson’s studio in Laurel Canyon after playing a run of small hootenannies there. But mostly it has to do with their sound, which has a warm, stripped-down Americana feel frequently described as “vintage.” Recently, the group got about as big a nod as four guys playing folk rock could hope for: Robbie Robertson, the somewhat reclusive songwriter from the Band, asked them to back him in a series of rare performances. Now in the middle of an East Coast tour to promote their follow-up record, “Nothing Is Wrong,” which was released this summer, Dawes seems both honored and amused to have been credited with leading a revival of the Laurel Canyon sound.

headline.main: The Weight

docs.abstract: How a generation that hated baby-boomer wistfulness can learn to do nostalgia right.
docs.snippet: How a generation that hated baby-boomer wistfulness can learn to do nostalgia right.
docs.lead_paragraph: Long before we had much life to look back on, North Americans my age knew that nostalgia was a sickness. It’s not that we were aware the term was coined to describe the crippling melancholia that overcame many 17th-century Swiss soldiers when war took them away from the bucolic mountain landscapes of home. It was that, being in our teens and 20s in the early 1990s, we had grown up in the penumbra of the great eclipsing nostalgia of the baby boomers, with their 1950s “Happy Days”; their 1960s (the Greatest Decade Ever Told); and their serial losses of innocence, via the Kennedys’ assassinations, Vietnam, Watergate, etc. — a record of revirginization to rival any evangelical chastity-pledge campaign.

docs.abstract: A New York architecture firm’s Hollywood installation pays tribute to Rem Koolhaas by playing with scales.
docs.snippet: A New York architecture firm’s Hollywood installation pays tribute to Rem Koolhaas by playing with scales.
docs.lead_paragraph: The New York architecture firm Lewis.Tsurumaki.Lewis (LTL) is taking up residence on Hollywood’s Walk of Fame with “4 Projects: 4 Scales,” a new exhibition at Woodbury University’s Hollywood outpost, at 6518 Hollywood Boulevard. Riffing on Rem Koolhaas’s iconic 1990s book “S, M, L, XL,” the exhibition focuses on projects that range in size from the micro to the massive, in a mix of built and speculative work. For the site-specific installation, LTL inserted a three-sided container with etched and printed surfaces into a long, narrow gallery space. Visitors entering the container make their way through the exhibition from the largest of the four projects on view to the smallest, walking on a white-painted wood floor that is laser-etched with the plans of each project. Canted walls of backlit panels provide photographs, architectural drawings and descriptive text. “Water Proving Ground,” at 69 million square feet, is LTL’s extra-large project. This visionary master plan for the northwest corner of New York Harbor was conceived as part of MoMA/P.S. 1’s recent “Rising Currents” initiative, which studied the impact of anticipated sea-level change on the city. The other projects in the show are all built works: Arthouse, a contemporary art center in Austin, Tex.; the Sullivan Family Student Center at the University of Wyoming in Laramie; and Lobby Wall, a site-specific sculpture for the lobby of Memorial Sloan-Kettering’s new Manhattan building, which is the smallest of the projects at 108 square feet.

headline.main: Seeing Things | Size Matters

docs.abstract: Bruce Smith’s tough-guy poems call attention to the male experience.
docs.snippet: Bruce Smith’s tough-guy poems call attention to the male experience.
docs.lead_paragraph: Bruce Smith’s new poems move fast and travel far, from Newtonian physics to the “fiery . . . riderless horse” of Christian apocalypse, “from the jet engine / as it gins the clouds” to “the hand-iron press and the sewing machine.” Most of those poems, though, begin in one place: a notion of blue-collar manhood, full of rough edges, frustration, defiance and pride. Smith’s Vietnam-era draftees, present-day stevedores, touring musicians and Iraq war veterans, along with their “black, white, sallow, olive, red, black kids,” inspire grand flights, tumultuous catalogs, as in a poem about drought: “Wherever there was water — the upended lid of a mayonnaise jar / in the gutter, the gutter, the sober silver puddle, the frenzied lake, / the tear ducts, the dew, the beveled rain — we drank.” When Smith is not speeding through such cascades of nouns, he revs up other repetitions: “They come like rats. . . . They want to save you. They want to slap you silly. They pet / the kitty. They bring gossip. . . . They’ve got questions for further study.” The plural noun to which each “They” refers is an obscenity most poets would not use.

headline.main: Poetry for Tough Guys

docs.lead_paragraph: Museum of the City of New York: ‘Whose Park is It? Financing and Administering New York’s New Parks’ (Tuesday) Creating and maintaining green spaces during a budget crunch is not exactly a walk in the park. An urban oasis designed today is very different from one designed in the days of Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux; you need only look at the High Line on the West Side of Manhattan, or Brooklyn Bridge Park, above, at the water’s edge in Brooklyn. A planned expansion there is expected to include several buildings of private housing — along with tennis courts, a swimming pool and other amenities — with payments from the buildings used to support the park’s operating expenses. On Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. Adrian Benepe, the New York parks commissioner, will discuss the history of the city’s parks and some issues surrounding park creation with Alexander D. Garvin, of the Yale School of Architecture, and Catherine Nagel, the executive director of the City Parks Alliance, an advocacy group based in Washington. Among the questions: Where will the money come from? What makes a park successful? The talk is part of an Urban Forum series at the museum (Fifth Avenue and 103rd Street) on the city’s infrastructure. It costs $12 ($8 for 65+ and students and $6 for members) and requires reservations: (917) 492-3395. Seating will be provided, so there’s no need for blankets or lawn chairs, and please, no picnics. For events at Brooklyn Bridge Park: brooklynbridgeparknyc.org. (Anne Mancuso)

docs.lead_paragraph: That American pastime of chopping cars is just one of the many true details that distinguish the seductive, grubby-beautiful, low-budget movie “Bellflower” from the usual indie chaff. The basic story sounds as dire as a quick read through a Sundance Film Festival catalog: Sensitive boy meets sexy girl. Happy and sad follow amid tears and beer, mumbled dialogue and openhearted sincerity, except that here they add up to an authentic slice of life, though one hopped up with an exuberant visual style and lurid excesses. Blood flows, fire belches, a devil car roars into the frame, and a couple meet cute over mouthfuls of live crickets.

docs.snippet: The Band of Heathens, a six-piece band from Austin, Tex., brought its tour in support of “Top Hat Crown & the Clapmaster’s Son” to Union Hall in Brooklyn.
docs.lead_paragraph: The air was getting thick downstairs at Union Hall in Brooklyn on Wednesday night, and the members of the Band of Heathens were making themselves at home. Ed Jurdi, seated at a keyboard, was belting a Southern soul number called “The Other Broadway,” in his high, tremulous rasp. Colin Brooks, at the other end of the stage, attacked his electric guitar, uncoiling blues licks in a coarsened tone. Between them was Gordy Quist, blithely strumming a rhythm-guitar riff. The band played the song and then extended it, pushing an ecstatic four-bar vamp, louder and wilder with each turnaround but without ceding any control.

docs.abstract: In his cabaret show at Feinstein’s, Jimmy Webb, a polished pop crooner, illustrated songs with his piano playing and his storytelling.
docs.snippet: In his cabaret show at Feinstein’s, Jimmy Webb, a polished pop crooner, illustrated songs with his piano playing and his storytelling.
docs.lead_paragraph: Jimmy Webb may have been performing his greatest hits for decades, but you could never call his show at Feinstein’s at Loews Regency on Wednesday evening an example of phoning it in. A more accurate description of his treatment of “By the Time I Get to Phoenix,” “Wichita Lineman,” “MacArthur Park” and “All I Know” would be impassioned deconstruction. There were many moments when Mr. Webb, who turns 65 on Aug. 15, suggested the singer-songwriter equivalent of a famished wolf howling in the wilderness. Instead of embracing the niceties of a polished pop crooner, he eviscerated his own songs, laying out their raw emotions — mostly a young man’s desperate romanticism — with such intensity that I wondered how anyone could feel so much.

headline.main: A Songwriter, Still on the Line

docs.abstract: A show at the Portland Museum of Art focuses on the last two decades of the life of John Marin, the acclaimed watercolorist often credited with influencing the Abstract Expressionists.
docs.snippet: A show at the Portland Museum of Art focuses on the last two decades of the life of John Marin, the acclaimed watercolorist often credited with influencing the Abstract Expressionists.
docs.lead_paragraph: The art of John Marin is easy to respect and hard to love. Compared with his vanguard associates of the between-the-wars era — Georgia O’Keeffe, Arthur Dove, Charles Demuth and Marsden Hartley — he was a flinty pragmatist. In the watercolors for which he was, and remains, most renowned, there is a hectic, sometimes luminously beautiful but often murky struggle between Cubist order and dynamic flux. Applied similarly to Manhattan cityscapes and Maine land- and seascapes, his touch is brusque, and his colors range from garish to drab. The invariably modest scale feels claustrophobic, despite the expansive subjects. Emotion is muted. An astringent pantheism is often suggested, but he was no visionary, and eros, whether carnal or mystical, is almost wholly absent.

headline.main: Testing the Waters of Abstraction

docs.lead_paragraph: A masterly tale about lives and stories and the art of their telling, “Mysteries of Lisbon” is also an elegiac meditation on love lost and rediscovered through misted memory. Directed by the Chilean filmmaker Raúl Ruiz and set mainly in Portugal, with detours to other European corners, it is a period picture based on a work by the prolific Camilo Castelo Branco (1825-90), who was born in Lisbon, illegitimate and orphaned, and flirted with the priesthood before finding his calling in writing, running off with a married woman, landing in prison and finally committing suicide. Mr. Ruiz’s “Mysteries” are just as outlandish, gloriously so.

docs.abstract: The Academy asks Brett Ratner to help produce the Oscars.
docs.snippet: The Academy asks Brett Ratner to help produce the Oscars.
docs.lead_paragraph: LOS ANGELES — If those who give the Oscars are looking for laughs, action and the occasional outrage from their annual awards show, they are on the right track. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences on Thursday said Brett Ratner, a filmmaker known for directing the raucous “Rush Hour” series and for producing “Horrible Bosses,” will join Don Mischer in producing the next Oscar show, which is set to air Feb. 26 on ABC. Last year’s broadcast, produced by Mr. Mischer and Bruce Cohen, had soft ratings and was widely criticized for a lackluster performance by one of its hosts, James Franco. If energy is the issue, Mr. Ratner should be able to provide a fix. He is known as a film aficionado and an ambitious filmmaker whose is currently making a Snow White project for Relativity Media, and has dozens of projects in development. Recently, Mr. Ratner directed “Tower Heist.” That action picture, due Nov. 4 from Universal Pictures, has uncertain Oscar prospects, but counts Ben Stiller, Eddie Murphy, Matthew Broderick and Gabourey Sidibe among its stars.

headline.main: Brett Ratner Takes Producing Role at the Oscars

docs.lead_paragraph: The guidebooks tell you never to tip in Japan. But when my partner and I traveled there last December, and our 90-pound bellhop insisted on carrying our overstuffed suitcases to our room, we thought a few hundred yen was more than appropriate. She politely refused our money. And over the course of the next week, so did the hotel clerks who equipped us with umbrellas at the first sign of drizzle, the concierges who booked us tables at mind-blowing sushi restaurants too off the grid to be listed on the Internet and the restaurant owners who presented us with a souvenir menu — in English — to commemorate all the delicious food we had just eaten. No tipping meant no tipping, period.

headline.main: Where to Get the World’s Best Service

docs.abstract: Does our 21st-century fascination with these hungry hordes stem from a general anxiety about overwhelming, uncontrollable threats?
docs.snippet: Does our 21st-century fascination with these hungry hordes stem from a general anxiety about overwhelming, uncontrollable threats?
docs.lead_paragraph: Zombies, traditionally, do not move with great speed or agility. As the sheriff in George A. Romero's classic 1968 movie, "Night of the Living Dead," astutely observes, “They’re dead, they’re all messed up.” But they’re also mighty persistent, and, apparently through sheer doggedness, the reanimated deceased have managed to occupy increasingly large areas of the popular imagination in the past few years. They don’t, of course, reproduce in the usual way. The Romero-type zombie, very much the dominant form these days, multiplies by contagion, like a virus: it feeds on flesh, and its bite is lethal, so even those semi-­fortunate humans who aren’t wholly devoured, but merely gnawed upon, die and come back as shuffling, hollow-­eyed flesh-­eaters themselves.

headline.main: The State of Zombie Literature: An Autopsy

Ricocheting in brief, staccato chapters among the perspectives of its main characters, Schwartz’s narrative depicted the shattering consequences of a hit-and-run accident on two Connecticut families. It ended with Dwight, the driver who killed a 10-year-old boy, about to confess to the police and go off to jail. But it also hinted that the families’ two surviving children — Dwight’s son, Sam, and the dead boy’s sister, Emma — would suffer the true emotional fallout of this tragedy.

docs.lead_paragraph: On April 8, 2009, the Maersk Alabama, a 17,000-ton United States cargo vessel, was hijacked by four Somali pirates several hundred miles east of Mogadishu. Bobbing in a lifeboat with the skipper, 53-year-old Richard Phillips, they began negotiating with the ship’s owners via cellphone for a multimillion-dollar ransom. For five days, the pirates and their hostage drifted in the Indian Ocean, shadowed by the U.S.S. Bainbridge, a destroyer that arrived at the scene not long after the hijacking. At dusk on April 12, Navy snipers killed three of the Somalis, and Phillips was rescued unharmed. The surviving pirate was seized and taken to the United States, where he pleaded guilty in a Manhattan courtroom to a host of charges and was sentenced to 33 years and nine months in a federal prison.

docs.lead_paragraph: WONDERFUL TOWN: Amor Towles, whose first novel, “Rules of Civility,” hits the hardcover fiction list at No. 16, arrived in New York in 1989 with diplomas from Yale and Stanford and dreams of becoming a writer. But he quickly noticed that all his friends who were waiting tables and pursuing art on the side looked just as tired as the office drones they were serving. So he joined an investment firm instead and took seven years off from writing. Towles, today a principal in a money management concern, says the novel’s success, though wonderful, has been less important than simply finishing something he thought was good. “I would’ve sold it for a penny, just to be able to say ‘O.K., I did it,’ ” he said in a telephone interview. “I always thought I was a writer on the inside, but after a few years of not writing you can’t make that claim anymore.”

docs.abstract: A series at Film Forum looks at Robert Ryan, a next-level star from the golden age who helped make the old Hollywood great.
docs.snippet: A series at Film Forum looks at Robert Ryan, a next-level star from the golden age who helped make the old Hollywood great.
docs.lead_paragraph: BORN to play beautifully tortured, angry souls, the actor Robert Ryan was a familiar movie face for more than two decades in Hollywood’s classical years, his studio ups and downs, independent detours and outlier adventures paralleling the arc of American cinema as it went from a national pastime to near collapse. A little prettier and he might have been one of the golden boys of the golden age. But there could be something a touch menacing about his face (something open and sweet too), which bunched as tight as a fist, and his towering height (he stood 6 foot 4) at times loomed like a threat. The rage boiled up in him so quickly. It made him seem dangerous.

headline.main: Robert Ryan’s Quiet Furies
headline.print_headline: Robert Ryan’s Quiet Furies

The reality program carried CBS to an overall ratings victory as well, averaging around 6.3 million total viewers for the night. docs.lead_paragraph: THERE has always been something erotically charged about elevators. The tightness of the space, the evocative enclosure, the tension arising from keeping one’s gaze from meeting another’s — all contribute to the frisson that can sometimes accompany a ride, even from the ground floor to the mezzanine. The following poems about elevators — and other modes of up-and-down conveyance, like stairs and escalators (which work on a different erotic principle) — were found last week in the Missed Connections section of newyork.craigslist.org. They are printed verbatim, with only line and stanza breaks added; their titles are the subject headings.

docs.lead_paragraph: Along the western edge of Hell’s Kitchen, nestled amid the many car dealerships is Print, an elegant farm-to-table restaurant in the lobby of Ink48, a Kimpton hotel in a former printing plant. The spot, at 48th Street and 11th Avenue, makes its own butter and limoncello and employs a full-time “forager” who travels the region and beyond to find fare like 3 Corner Field Farm lamb and Battenkill Valley Creamery milk. A rarity in the neighborhood, it has become something of a go-to place for people who work at Kenneth Cole, Prada, Coach and Ogilvy & Mather, all of which have offices nearby. On Tuesday evening, the crowd included two business associates catching up.

docs.lead_paragraph: Fannie Mae, the mortgage-finance company under government conservatorship, reported a $2.9 billion second-quarter loss on Friday and said it would seek $5.1 billion in Treasury Department aid to balance its books. Fannie Mae requested the money to eliminate a net worth deficit of $5.1 billion for the three-month period that ended June 30, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing by the company, which is based in Washington. The loss, which compares with a $1.2 billion loss a year earlier, was mostly a result of credit-related expenses on home loans made before the 2008 financial collapse. Fannie Mae also made a $2.3 billion payment to the Treasury in the second quarter. As of the second quarter, Fannie Mae has drawn $104.8 billion in Treasury aid and paid $14.7 billion in dividends, the company reported. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac together have drawn about $170 billion in taxpayer aid.

docs.lead_paragraph: Following in the footsteps of Vivien Leigh, Cate Blanchett and Marge Simpson, Nicole Ari Parker (“Soul Food”) has landed the role of Blanche DuBois in the coming Broadway production of Tennessee Williams’s classic drama “A Streetcar Named Desire,” the producers announced Sunday. It will be Ms. Parker’s Broadway debut; she previously performed in Off Broadway productions of “Chicago,” “House of Lear” and “Romeo and Juliet.” A graduate of the Tisch School for the Performing Arts, Ms. Parker described the news as “a childhood dream come true.” She added: “Blanche is the role of a lifetime. When I heard, I spun around in my kitchen like Diana Ross in ‘The Wiz.’ ” The production, which will feature a cast representative of the play’s New Orleans setting, is to open in the spring under the direction of Emily Mann (“Anna in the Tropics,” “Having Our Say”) and starring Blair Underwood (“The Event”). Mr. Underwood will also be making his Broadway debut, as Stanley Kowalski.

docs.abstract: It has been raining at the festival. And the main stage, where there is no tent for the audience, has it the hardest.
docs.snippet: It has been raining at the festival. And the main stage, where there is no tent for the audience, has it the hardest.
docs.lead_paragraph: NEWPORT, R.I. — Since the beginning of the Newport Jazz Festival on Sunday it has been raining, sometimes hard and loud and overwhelming, sometimes a thick harborside mist. The main stage, where there is no tent for the audience, has it the hardest. Maybe 150 hardy people are out there right now watching James Farm, the co-operative quartet with the saxophonist Joshua Redman, the pianist Aaron Parks, the bassist Matt Penman and the drummer Eric Harland. They’re playing way back from the lip of the stage to avoid getting wet, huddling closer than they would at a small club. They’re sounding good–strolling, right now, through a minor ballad.Hiromi is back for round two on a smaller stage with her trio, wowing them with amiable virtuosity. Earlier, John Hollenbeck’s 19-piece big band– including bass saxophone, vibraphone and two singers– played a great set, including songs by Ornette Coleman, Jimmy Webb and Imogen Heap and a version of the traditional “I’m a Man of Constant Sorrow,” with a solo by the tenor saxophonist Tony Malaby that came in chapters, getting destabilized and righting itself, using a few notes of the melody or, or of Hollenbeck’s strong arrangement, to start a new section. It takes at least a half-hour to start to understand this band’s range, from sci-fi to pastoral, loopy to dead serious. It’s come a long way over the last 10 years.

headline.main: At Newport, Rain Rules the Day

docs.abstract: Toward the end of summer every year, we get a surge in inquiries from the State Department, the Army, the Marines. We actually sell a low percentage of these calls.
docs.snippet: Toward the end of summer every year, we get a surge in inquiries from the State Department, the Army, the Marines. We actually sell a low percentage of these calls.
docs.lead_paragraph: The end of summer brings a surge in calls from government clients, mostly from the military, looking to spend remaining dollars in their budgets before the fiscal year ends on Oct. 1. This year is no exception. The surge has started and is most likely to peak at the end of August. Just last week we got calls from the State Department, the Army and the Marines. The person on the phone is generally a low-level officer, responding to a request from a superior for pricing on a large and fancy table. Our bid will be presented to the upper ranks as one of a number of ways to spend their remaining money. Consequently, we sell a much lower percentage of these inquiries than those from private clients. But August is usually a slower month for private business, so we take the time to write proposals anyway.

headline.main: The Government’s Calling About a Table. Should I Take the Call?

docs.abstract: In trying to marry the prissiness of the Victorians with the sexual revolution of the 1960s, Tabitha Simmons has come out with an English heritage collection that is a hybrid hoot.
docs.snippet: In trying to marry the prissiness of the Victorians with the sexual revolution of the 1960s, Tabitha Simmons has come out with an English heritage collection that is a hybrid hoot.
docs.lead_paragraph: In trying to marry the prissiness of the Victorians with the sexual revolution of the 1960s, Tabitha Simmons has come out with an English heritage collection that is a hybrid hoot. “Like rockabilly shoes,” the English designer says of her inspirations, “but — more gothic.” The 49 styles are indeed evocative of the British Isles, with a smattering of high-heel brogues, evening sandals with chandelier trim and suede boots that look like they stepped out of “Bedknobs and Broomsticks.” Compared to previous collections, it is slightly more macabre, yet Simmons, now in her fifth season, continues to demonstrate an ability to imbue classic styles with a modern twist. For example, the Edna heel, a reimagined stiletto loafer, “is beetle-crusher when it’s in black and white,” she says, “and then we did a red and leopard version that has an element of Victoriana.” She’s certainly got a bead on the new monarchy. A pair of nude silk slippers looks fit for a duchess or a Park Avenue princess.

headline.main: The Red Shoes Are Coming

docs.abstract: Bras and panties in tandem styles: so French, so chic.
docs.snippet: Bras and panties in tandem styles: so French, so chic.
docs.lead_paragraph: It started when my very Parisian friend, staying at my New York apartment, hand-washed her lingerie and neatly hung the coordinating pairs along the shower rod. Bras and panties in tandem styles: frilly florals by Only Hearts, nude sheers from Eres and a hot pink number that could have only been from Agent Provocateur. So French, so chic. I squirmed in my mismatched red cotton briefs and orange satin bra. Why had it never dawned on me to match? “I only started buying sets when I got married,” says the author and Vogue contributing editor Plum Sykes, remembering a pistachio and cream lace combo she fell in love with on the Rue des Saints-Pères in Paris. “Young women today seem to be more aware of the trend for beautiful matching lingerie,” says Cynthia Gabay, Myla’s creative director. “Your underpinnings say as much about you as a person as your choice in clothing or accessories.” My early-20-something self now officially desires grown-up glamour — and one trip to Bergdorf’s later, taps and teddies are joined at the hip.

headline.main: Match.com

docs.lead_paragraph: VALENTINE, Neb. — The nearest ocean is a thousand miles away. Yet across central Nebraska, peeking out from rolling hills of prairie grass, is sand — beige and reminiscent of a Caribbean beach. Nebraska’s sandhills are the largest sand dunes in North America, spreading for more than 20,000 square miles, over more than a quarter of the state. The sand hails from the Rocky Mountains: tiny specks of eroded quartz that blew east and landed here, 8,000 years ago.

docs.lead_paragraph: For its fall collection of icicle-drop necklaces and pendants, Kora, the L.A.-based, African-made jewelry line, teamed up with glass makers in the Kenyan village of Kitengela. A mere two years old, Kora has dedicated itself to creating “trade not aid” jobs by designing and marketing hand-fashioned pieces made from recycled bone, aluminum, brass, horn and now glass. ”The colors of the glowing green glass are incredible; it’s so unlike animal horn,” says Kora’s co-founder Maxandra Short (above, left). Her partner, Amy Walker, adds, “Glass necklaces still have an organic feel, because every piece is different.” Indeed the latest offerings, like the necklace at right ($220; go to koradesigns.com), are a softer addition to the line’s usually more brawny designs, which in the past have included tribal-inspired manacles and industrial-looking chains. “I think we’re even going to be playing with color in bone,“ Walker says. “Color is our thing now.”

headline.main: Coup de Glass

docs.abstract: Why we humans seem to want for little but are craving nonstop.
docs.snippet: Why we humans seem to want for little but are craving nonstop.
docs.lead_paragraph: Feeling low? According to a new study in the Journal of Consumer Research, when people feel bad, their sense of touch quickens and they instinctively want to hug something or someone. Tykes cling to a teddy bear or blanket. It’s a mammal thing. If young mammals feel gloomy, it’s usually because they’re hurt, sick, cold, scared or lost. So their brain rewards them with a gust of pleasure if they scamper back to mom for a warm nuzzle and a meal. No need to think it over. All they know is that, when a negative mood hits, a cuddle just feels right; and if they’re upbeat and alert, then their eyes hunger for new sights and they’re itching to explore.

headline.main: Evolution’s Gold Standard
headline.print_headline: Evolution’s Gold Standard

docs.abstract: Some thoughts on the downgrade of American debt by Standard & Poor’s.
docs.snippet: Some thoughts on the downgrade of American debt by Standard & Poor’s.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s hard not to feel a certain contempt for Standard & Poor’s in the wake of its downgrade of American debt. Its sole job as a credit-rating agency is to gauge the creditworthiness of bonds, yet like its competitors, Moody’s and Fitch, it has consistently fallen short. It downgraded Enron days before the company went bankrupt. Its willingness to slap a AAA rating on securitized subprime junk was the foundation upon which the entire financial crisis was built. And now, to show that it’s got some spine, S.& P. decided to downgrade the United States? From a purely economic standpoint, the likelihood of a U.S. default is nil. As my friend Daniel Alpert, a founding managing partner of Westwood Capital, put it: “The size of the U.S. economy, the wealth of its inhabitants and the assets of the sovereign entity itself are unquestionably more than adequate to repay, with interest, all of the $14 trillion or so of the nation’s debt.” He added, “Anyone with a rudimentary understanding of finance and economics can figure that out.” On Monday, with the market collapsing, where did investors rush to put their money? In the one security they still considered safe: U.S. Treasuries.

docs.lead_paragraph: THIS year I took Highway 80 from Montgomery to Selma, Ala., reversing the journey of activists in three separate civil rights marches in March 1965. (He runs on J-shaped prosthetics made of black carbon fiber and has been dubbed the “Blade Runner.”) Mr. Pistorius, shown shirtless and running at full speed, has started appearing in ads for a new fragrance from Thierry Mugler. Now, Juliet Macur reports in today’s Sports section of The Times that Mr. Pistorius has achieved another milestone in his athletic career: He has been named to South Africa’s team for the track and field world championships, which will make him the first amputee to compete at the event. Ms. Macur reports that he will race in the 400 meters and 4 x 400 relay.

headline.main: Another Breakthrough for Oscar Pistorius

docs.abstract: More photos of the Henan restaurant Uncle Zhou in Queens, the subject of this week’s $25 and Under.
docs.snippet: More photos of the Henan restaurant Uncle Zhou in Queens, the subject of this week’s $25 and Under.
docs.lead_paragraph: This is not your father’s Hunan restaurant. Uncle Zhou (pronounced Uncle Joe) features the cuisine of Henan, breadbasket of China, especially the province’s well-known wheat noodles. Knife-shaved noodles are brusquely cut from a lump of dough, boiled until wonderfully chewy, and deposited in cool bowls dressed with tomato and egg. Thin, hand-pulled noodles swirl at the bottom of spicy soups; their ribbonlike cousins are great for swabbing the plate. Other are stretched to the fineness of angel hair, baked, then deposited as a crisp thatch atop a whole fish, swimming in a pool of sweet-and-sour sauce. Noodles and fish soak up the sauce; you and your friends soak up the lively atmosphere.

headline.main: Reviewing Uncle Zhou

docs.snippet: “The Help,” Tate Taylor’s movie set in civil-rights-era Mississippi, shifts between black maids and their employers.
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s a scene in “The Help,” the new movie based on Kathryn Stockett’s novel, that cracks open the early-’60s world of strained smiles and gentility that rarely leaps out of this big, ole slab of honey-glazed hokum. It’s after hours, and Aibileen, a maid played with determined grace by Viola Davis, is going home. Suddenly the bus stops, and a white man orders the black passengers off, explaining that a black man has been shot — except that he doesn’t say black, Negro or colored. In a pool of dreadful night, Aibileen and a young man trade goodbyes and rush off. And then this sturdy, frightened woman starts running as if her life were in danger, because it’s Mississippi, and it is.

headline.main: ‘The Maids’ Now Have Their Say

He and his assistants then began creating installations on the property that, at least to judge from this movie, are a monument to the human will to self-annihilation and a rehearsal for the apocalypse.

docs.abstract: A tone poem of gridlock — car horns, screeching brakes, revving motorcycles — plays daily in SoHo near the entrance to the Holland Tunnel.
docs.snippet: A tone poem of gridlock — car horns, screeching brakes, revving motorcycles — plays daily in SoHo near the entrance to the Holland Tunnel.
docs.lead_paragraph: A red-white-and-blue sign at the corner of West Broadway and Watts Street in SoHo reads, “Don’t Honk — $350 Penalty.” It is, shall we say, not always heeded. This corner is a five-way crossing, where Broome Street forks into Watts, which leads to the Holland Tunnel, and crosses West Broadway, which has two-way traffic. The tunnel entrances themselves run smoothly, if slowly; traffic police officers are there. But the New Jersey exodus has to back up somewhere, and this corner is one of those places. Amid this gridlock is a whole lot of self-expression via car horns and the occasional, ah, verbal admonition.

headline.main: The Contrapuntal Sounds of Gridlock

docs.lead_paragraph: The Los Angeles City Council on Tuesday unanimously approved a tentative agreement with a private developer to build a $1.2 billion football stadium, in hopes of attracting an N.F.L. team back to downtown. The terms of the agreement with the developer, Anschutz Entertainment Group, allow for the demolition and relocation of part of the Los Angeles Convention Center to make room for the 72,000-seat stadium, which could open as soon as 2016. The city’s approval of the downtown stadium plan is a blow to a competing plan to build a N.F.L. stadium in the nearby City of Industry. Anschutz Entertainment Group has promised to finance the stadium and two parking lots without any cost to Los Angeles taxpayers. Over the next nine months, the City Council will negotiate terms and then vote on final approval.

headline.main: California: Los Angeles Stadium Plan Is Approved
headline.print_headline: California: Los Angeles Stadium Plan Is Approved

docs.abstract: Shipping unused medical equipment to poor hospitals is a great idea, but it has to be done right.
docs.snippet: Shipping unused medical equipment to poor hospitals is a great idea, but it has to be done right.
docs.lead_paragraph: In Friday’s Fixes column I wrote about organizations that collect usable surplus equipment and supplies from hospitals in the United States and ship it to hospitals that need them in poor countries.   Readers were generally enthusiastic about the environmental and health benefits of this idea, but some offered important cautions. Homira from Wash, D.C. (15) wrote:  “There are a slew of complex issues that make donations of any kind aside from financial  really poor practice for trying to help developing countries. When it comes to medical equipment donations, the consumables necessary to operate many of these machines, such as x-ray film, reagents, etc,  are often not considered prior to the donations; nor is life-cycle costing and maintenance and operational costing and support figured in. Subsequently we see a lot of discarded medical equipment lying around clinics, hospitals and dump sites in low-income countries we work in.”

headline.main: Making Medical Donations Work

docs.lead_paragraph: For years the domed structure between the Aya Sofia (Hagia Sophia) and the Blue Mosque was used as a state-run carpet shop. Kilims and halis were strewn every which way across marble navel stones under huge domes that let shafts of light illuminate the structure built in 1556 by the famed architect Sinan to house the baths of Roxelana, known locally as Hurrem. Now, thanks to a $10 million restoration, the marble-clad space is once again a Turkish bath house, with separate facilities for men and women.

headline.main: High-End Hamam Opens in Historic Istanbul Location

She was 45 and pregnant after six years of fertility bills, ovulation injections, donor eggs and disappointment — and yet here she was, 14 weeks into her pregnancy, choosing to extinguish one of two healthy fetuses, almost as if having half an abortion. docs.snippet: All the right people have come to know First Aid Kit, a Swedish folk duo made up of the sisters Johanna and Klara Soderberg.
docs.lead_paragraph: In indie rock, it’s not so much who you know as who knows you. And all the right people have come to know First Aid Kit, a Swedish folk duo made up of the sisters Johanna (left) and Klara Söderberg. They were discovered by Karin Dreijer Andersson (one half of the Swedish sibling duo the Knife), who released their first EP. They met Conor Oberst on the Monsters of Folk tour in Sweden; he introduced them to the producer of their next album. When First Aid Kit passed through Nashville on their American tour, Jack White invited them to record for his label. Part of a proud folk tradition — they “enjoy singing older songs,” Johanna says — they chose to rework Buffy Sainte-Marie’s “Universal Soldier,” a protest song from the ’60s, whose message “is unfortunately still very relevant today.”

headline.main: Timely | Northern Lights

docs.snippet: Fishing lessons provided by New England’s old timers.
docs.lead_paragraph: I love fishing, which was one of the ways, growing up in Rhode Island, that I developed my broader passion for the wider living world outside of the human-built one. As a kid paddling around in a dinghy, I could “feel” the otherwise invisible seabed by bouncing my weighted hand line off the bottom. While waiting for a bite fishing for mackerel from a floating dock, I’d stick my head down close to the water and peer at the fascinating assemblage of small shrimp, sea squirts and other creatures growing on the immersed wood and floats.

docs.lead_paragraph: The premise of Dr. Nassir Ghaemi’s book about leadership and mental illness is simple. It need not be reiterated as frequently as Dr. Ghaemi repeats it. But he begins “A First-Rate Madness” by writing, “This book argues that in at least one vitally important circumstance insanity produces good results and sanity is a problem.” To put it only a shade differently: “When our world is in tumult, mentally ill leaders function best.” Or: “In the storm of crisis, complete sanity can steer us astray, while some insanity brings us to port.”

docs.lead_paragraph: SANTA FE, N.M. — Vivaldi would surely find it frustrating, if not a little strange, that his achievement as a composer today is distorted by the cultlike popularity of “The Four Seasons.” He was indeed a master of Baroque instrumental music. Still, from his early days he was powerfully drawn to the theater and to the voice. He wrote nearly 50 operas. Yet productions are rare. The mezzo-soprano Cecilia Bartoli brought overdue attention to Vivaldi’s operas with a successful album of arias in 1999 and a subsequent concert tour.

docs.abstract: While we dally in the off-season, how does one find (and love) things to buy now?
docs.snippet: While we dally in the off-season, how does one find (and love) things to buy now?
docs.lead_paragraph: Like many women nowadays, I shop for my bikinis in the snow and boots in the blistering heat. You could say I’ve adapted. There is a despairing time lapse between when collections are shown (spring in September and fall in February) and when those pieces are sold. (Fall hits stores as early as July, and spring in February.) And thanks to instantaneous gratification sites like Moda Operandi and Gilt Groupe, avid customers can now begin preordering directly from their favorite designers. “I start planning the moment they walk down the runway,” says the designer Margherita Missoni. But some months, like September, linger in a sort of shopping purgatory. The idea of scouring the racks while waiting for sales and holiday items to hit the floor seems outdated. And tired. So while we dally in the off-season, how does one find (and love) things to buy now?

headline.main: The September Issue

docs.lead_paragraph: Dirk Schoenberger walks into the lobby of the Bowery Hotel wearing Prada’s infamous platform espadrille wingtips — an odd choice considering that Schoenberger is the creative director of the sports style division at Adidas, a company known for its footwear. What he likes about the Pradas, he explains, is “the mix of sharp tailoring and casual leisure.” Having held his post for little over a year, he has pushed Adidas to hybridize in a similar manner. “When I’m in Berlin and I see how the young guys and girls are dressing, none of them are wearing sneakers anymore. So you think, if these are the target consumers, and we are only selling sneakers, well, what are we going to do?” The answer may be found in Adidas SLVR. Priced somewhere between Originals and Y-3 (also under Schoenberger’s purview), the line has been reimagined for fall under his personal design stewardship. “It’s amazing for such a big company to be so open for discussions,” he says. With SLVR, it is a “new approach but still very much in the language of Adidas.”

headline.main: Silver Lining

docs.abstract: The decision is part of the ongoing fallout from a legal dispute that has halted all loans from Russian to American museums.
docs.snippet: The decision is part of the ongoing fallout from a legal dispute that has halted all loans from Russian to American museums.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Metropolitan Museum of Art has officially canceled plans to loan works by the fashion designer Paul Poiret to Moscow’s Kremlin Museum, as part of the ongoing fallout from a legal dispute that has halted all loans from Russian to American museums. “It’s really a matter of fairness and equity,” the Met’s spokesman, Harold Holzer, said. As long as Russia’s “loan embargo is in place,” Mr. Holzer said, “this museum believes it can no longer lend to Russian museums.” The Met was to lend 35 Poiret works to the show, which is scheduled to open at the Moscow museum on September 6. The cancellation of the loans was first reported by the New York Observer.

headline.main: Met Cancels Plans to Loan Works to Moscow’s Kremlin Museum

docs.lead_paragraph: Soon after I finished my surgical training, I worked with a young doctor who was impressive not only for his clinical skills but also for his devotion to patients. He was large and powerfully built but never seemed to loom over his patients, miraculously shrinking down to their eye level whenever he spoke with them. He listened intently to every detail of their travails and always ended the visits by asking if they still had any unanswered questions.

headline.main: Letting Doctors Make the Tough Decisions

docs.lead_paragraph: At Les Arts Decoratifs in Paris, the summer crowds have gravitated to the Hussein Chalayan show and the exhibition of highlights from Ralph Lauren’s car collection. I was glad to see both on a recent trip, but I was also lucky to spot a sign for another, less-heralded exhibition at the museum. “Plastique Ludique” (“Playful Plastic”), which runs until Nov. 6, presents the work of the Czech toy designer Libuse Niklova (1934-1981), whose work with plastics, particularly in the 1960s and ’70s, changed the look — and the nature — of toys in her native country. Niklova believed that children should be able to play as creatively as possible, and the development of plastics after World War II offered a helpful tool. Her inflatable buffalo, giraffe and elephant, with their simplified, graphic silhouettes and bright, pop colors, could be used as chairs or pool toys for small children. (The three have been reissued in limited numbers and are for sale at the museum’s shop.) And Niklova’s ingenious use of pleated plastic piping produced animals with accordion-like midsections that squealed when squeezed. In contrast to the Chalayan and Lauren exhibitions, which are about the more expensive pleasures of the material world, “Plastique Ludique” offers a surprising, refreshing look at a more modest — yet no less inventive — endeavor.

headline.main: Now Playing | Plastique Ludique

docs.lead_paragraph: In Boston, scientists measuring the city’s greenhouse gas emissions have found what they call a “weekend effect,” a clear drop-off in the amount of carbon dioxide entering the city’s atmosphere on Saturdays and Sundays. In Fresno, researchers have discovered that backyard water use increases with wealth, as does backyard biodiversity. And in Los Angeles, ecologists studying the city’s “ecohydrology” have calculated that planting a million new trees, an idea with fairly universal appeal, would have the drawback of increasing water consumption by 5 percent.

headline.main: As Ecosystems, Cities Yield Some Surprises

docs.abstract: A love letter to Auto-Tune in several parts.
docs.snippet: A love letter to Auto-Tune in several parts.
docs.lead_paragraph: One thing you learn when you spend a bunch of time on YouTube looking up songs that use the electronic pitch-correction algorithm known as Auto-Tune is that a lot of people really hate Auto-Tune. Which is weird. It’s just a sound — obnoxious in the hands of the untalented, occasionally amazing in the hands of the amazing. Hating it is like hating falsettos, or the accordion. And, O.K., given the current omnipresence of the sound in pop music, it’s like hating the accordion during some strange period of accordion-fascism during which everyone’s paying top dollar to sound like early Los Lobos or Weird Al. Rap and R&B may have run with Auto-Tune more than other genres, but these days you can’t get away from it, even by listening to metal, country or Moroccan music.

headline.main: Really Now, What’s So Bad About Auto-Tune Pop?

docs.abstract: Thanks to a waterfront renovation, a sleek new tram system, a first wave of design hotels and a generation of young restaurant and night-life impresarios, Marseille is looking better than ever.
docs.snippet: Thanks to a waterfront renovation, a sleek new tram system, a first wave of design hotels and a generation of young restaurant and night-life impresarios, Marseille is looking better than ever.
docs.lead_paragraph: FIRST the bad news: Marseille is not Paris. Unlike its culture-rich rival, France’s second-largest city has no world-class museums, must-see monuments or internationally renowned chefs. Now the good news: Marseille is not Paris. Kissed by the Mediterranean, Marseille can claim an un-Parisian combination of near-constant sun, miles of beaches and an ethnic mix — French, North African, Italian, Corsican, Armenian — that lends a flavor unlike anywhere else in the country. No wonder the rest of France calls it Planète Mars. And the news gets better: Named a European Capital of Culture for 2013, the historically gritty port is looking up, thanks to a waterfront renovation, a sleek new tram system, a first wave of design hotels, a generation of young restaurant and night-life impresarios and a homegrown fashion scene. More than ever, there is life on Mars.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Marseille

docs.lead_paragraph: In Los Angeles, everyone’s a hybrid. Caterer-dancer. Shop girl-singer. Bartender-drama student. Take Justin Kern: model, screenwriter and now fashion designer. Kern and his partner, Stephanie Danan, film producer and fashion designer, have founded Co, a collection of luxurious mega-basics: slip dresses, silk tanks and skirts, L.B.D.’s, skinny leather pants and the kind of big old fancy furs that Margot Tenenbaum would adore. The Royal Tenenbaum, in fact, is the personification of the Co customer — a woman who pictures herself in a variety of cinematic situations. To illuminate this idea, Kern and Danan (far right) collaborated with the actress Élodie Bouchez and the director Thomas Bangalter of Daft Punk on a four-minute film that they describe as a period piece with a sci-fi twist. (The film will have its premiere on T’s Web site during Fashion Week.) “We wanted to give the clothes an identity through the characters that we imagine inhabiting them,” Danan says. Margot, fictional character-muse, are you listening?

headline.main: Compound Interest

docs.lead_paragraph: Andrew Rice did a wonderful job in “Life on the Line” describing the misunderstood binational bubble that is El Paso, Tex., and Juárez, Mexico. His picture is incomplete, however. Virtually every one of the sources he quoted was someone who had more than enough money to pay for an investor’s visa or take other measures to flee the violence in Mexico and remake their lives on the U.S. side with very little disturbance to their family life. But what about the hundreds of thousands of poor Juarenses who escape with nothing more than the clothes on their backs and horrible stories haunting them? It’s not so easy. There are no visas to keep them safe, no work permits, and the U.S. government is reluctant to give them asylum, granting less than 2 percent of petitions from Mexican nationals.

docs.lead_paragraph: Sometimes I feel as though I’ve written more words about Harry Potter than has J. K. Rowling herself. I reviewed installments in the movie series for two different newspapers. I assembled two separate Internet slide shows ranking all of the films. I led multiple book clubs about Harry Potter novels — one, discussing the sixth book, over e-mail with friends, and the other, about the seventh book, in an online magazine. I narrated a video critiquing Daniel Radcliffe’s acting. I penned blog posts on Good Snape versus Bad Snape. I mashed up Harry Potter with Tony Soprano. I created Ron Weasley’s Facebook page. I wrote an obituary for Hedwig the owl. I visited the Wizarding World of Harry Potter and whined publicly that it wasn’t magical enough. I wrote about Dumbledore coming out, Antonin Scalia’s resemblance to Snape and copyright-violating Asian knockoff books with titles like “Harry Potter and the Filler of Big.”

docs.lead_paragraph: There was once a time, centuries before Internet shopping, when buyers and sellers could honorably carry out their exchanges without ever meeting. In the gold-for-salt commerce of Saharan and Sahel tribes, for example, the Saharans would leave a salt pile by the banks of the Niger, then remove themselves so their clients could, in seclusion, deposit a sum of gold. At that point, the merchants would return, but if the payment was deemed insufficient, they would leave it with the salt and withdraw. The Sahel merchants would approach again, and this good-faith dance of advance and retreat would be repeated until both parties felt content with the deal.

docs.abstract: The titanic success of George R. R. Martin’s gritty “Song of Ice and Fire” series has swept away the traditional “aren’t we a little old for this?” view of fantasy.
docs.snippet: The titanic success of George R. R. Martin’s gritty “Song of Ice and Fire” series has swept away the traditional “aren’t we a little old for this?” view of fantasy.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s a high time for high fantasy. Novels about wizards outsell (and often outshine) the most glittering literary fiction titles; the contemporary romantic hero generally sports a pair of fangs; and even now the five remaining earthlings who haven’t read “The Lord of the Rings” are being hunted down and put to the sword. Yet for all of fantasy’s successes, there remains a chip on the spaulder of the genre. As Michael Agger put it in 2009, reviewing Lev Grossman’s Harry Potter-­influenced novel “The Magicians”: “Perhaps a fantasy novel meant for adults can’t help being a strange mess of effects. . . . Sounds like fun, but aren’t we a little old for this?” And with that, hundreds of years of fantastical writing are reduced to 20-­sided dice, pencil nubs, half-filled Coke cans and the crushing realization that no, your elven rogue’s dagger is not going to be effective against green slime.

headline.main: Dragons Ascendant: George R. R. Martin and the Rise of Fantasy

docs.abstract: Lisa Appignanesi examines the “unruly emotion” of love and its impact throughout the course of our lives.
docs.snippet: Lisa Appignanesi examines the “unruly emotion” of love and its impact throughout the course of our lives.
docs.lead_paragraph: The news about love — if anything can be said to be new when it comes to love — is that it affects us on more levels than we realized. Poets and artists have long viewed love as a prime mover, but by the beginning of the last century, scientists and philosophers were dismissing it as socially and scientifically irrelevant. Love was confined to private life, where only women and novelists and psychoanalysts were supposed to pay much attention to it. Then, a little more than half a century ago, biologists and economists and psychologists decided that love mattered after all, and began conducting experiments to determine how much.

docs.abstract: Simon Reynolds laments how pop culture feeds on its own history, borrowing from a past that is ever more immediate.
docs.snippet: Simon Reynolds laments how pop culture feeds on its own history, borrowing from a past that is ever more immediate.
docs.lead_paragraph: Five years ago, a young Scottish woman named Sandi Thom reached No. 1 on the British charts with her song “I Wish I Was a Punk Rocker (With Flowers in My Hair).” She delivered it with a voice of pleading and with a cappella sincerity, as if she were trying to sell you something. Perhaps that was why I found it irritating; or else it was the suggestion that punk rockers would break bread with someone who had flowers in her hair. Thanks to Simon Reynolds’s “Retromania,” I now understand that she “purposefully conflated 1967 and 1977 to speak to the vague nostalgia felt by many young people for a lost golden age when music had power and integrity.”

docs.snippet: Isaac Osei, who owns a taxi fleet in New York City with his wife, is also a Ghanaian chief who wears a crown and oversees five towns.
docs.lead_paragraph: BEFORE dawn, when most New Yorkers are fast asleep, Isaac and Elizabeth Osei have already been working for hours. On a recent morning, Mr. Osei drove his wife from New Jersey to the half-abandoned outer blocks of Midtown Manhattan to oversee the 4:30 a.m. transfer of their fleet of 50 taxis. With Ms. Osei leading the way and a sliver of moon still hanging in the sky, they scouted three square blocks to make sure all of their taxis had been picked up by drivers. Then, over the screeches emanating from auto-body shops and the smell of gasoline wafting from a Hess station crammed with cabs, they surveyed their troubled taxis just as sunlight faintly appeared over Manhattan.

docs.snippet: Lorene Cary’s latest novel explores a family’s struggle involving race and inheritance in the South.
docs.lead_paragraph: It takes less than a day to drive from Philadelphia to Beaufort County, S.C., but to Alonzo Rayne, the 30-year-old protagonist of “If Sons, Then Heirs,” the journey spans more than a hundred years. From the very start of Lorene Cary’s latest novel, when Rayne sets off to visit Nana Selma, the great-­grandmother who raised him, he’s enveloped by a sense of home. Taking along his girlfriend’s 7-year-old son, Rayne has high hopes for what the trip will give the boy: “How good it would be for him to have the experience of earlier generations, to spend time in a rural setting, to know from their own experience that black people . . . owned land and barns and silos, that they had rights to water from creeks and streams.”

docs.snippet: The characters in Amor Towles’s first novel try to reinvent themselves in 1930s New York.
docs.lead_paragraph: The saying “May you live in interesting times” has undeniable resonance for the investment executive-turned-­novelist Amor Towles. In 1989, he was set to go to China for two years to teach. When the Tiananmen Square massacre put an abrupt end to that plan, he headed for Manhattan. On his first night in the city, he met two strangers. One would become his brother-in-law; through the other, he found the job in which he has worked for 20 years. What would have happened if he’d hit town a day later? This is the kind of improbable-but-true serendipity that plots the lives of people in their 20s — in whatever epoch — before they know the weight that decisions made in a moment might have.

docs.abstract: Can a literary vegetarian from Brooklyn unite what basketball has torn asunder? Why else would Duke and the University of North Carolina have assigned Jonathan Safran Foer’s “Eating Animals” to all incoming freshmen?
docs.snippet: Can a literary vegetarian from Brooklyn unite what basketball has torn asunder? Why else would Duke and the University of North Carolina have assigned Jonathan Safran Foer’s “Eating Animals” to all incoming freshmen?
docs.lead_paragraph: REQUIRED READING: Can a peaceable literary vegetarian from Brooklyn bring together what a bloody Southern basketball rivalry has torn asunder? That was surely the hope of administrators at Duke and the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, when they chose Jonathan Safran Foer’s “Eating Animals” as the joint summer reading for this fall’s incoming freshmen. So far, the carnivore-unfriendly choice does not seem to have elicited any complaints from the local barbecue industry, though the state’s educators have courted controversy before. In 2002, conservative pundits and state legislators howled when U.N.C. assigned Michael Sells’s “Approaching the Qur’an,” calling it an insult to the memory of Sept. 11. In 2003, a student group called The Committee for a Better Carolina denounced that year’s choice, Barbara Ehrenreich’s “Nickel and Dimed,” as a “classic Marxist rant” and “intellectual pornography with no redeeming characteristics.”

docs.abstract: I didn’t want to fall for another of-the-moment shoe. But let’s call it the one that got away.
docs.snippet: I didn’t want to fall for another of-the-moment shoe. But let’s call it the one that got away.
docs.lead_paragraph: Call them the ones that got away. Spring 2009: Ann Demeulemeester’s open-toe lace-up heels came down the runway and the quiet, almost suspicious stirring that precedes a full-blown frenzy began. Everyone wanted them. And, why wouldn’t they: hefty heel, combat-boot-like lacing that left just the right amount of skin showing, options in black or brown leather. But despite the hype — countless credits in fashion magazines, followed by colleagues professing how comfortable they were while wearing them with everything from jean shorts to Sunday dresses — I didn’t buy a pair. My reason (aside from the $965 price tag)? I wasn’t going to let myself fall for another of-the-moment shoe.

headline.main: All Consuming | The Ann Demeulemeester Lace-Up Heel

docs.lead_paragraph: To the Editor: Re the Practical Traveler column (July 31): Having traveled abroad a number of times, I have sought methods to avoid incurring large expenses when getting vaccines. Many travel clinics charge more than $80 for a consult as their vaccine prices are often artificially inflated (Havrix for hepatitis A has a wholesale price of about $73, not $90). I typically read mdtravelhealth.com to find out what vaccines I need, ask my primary care doctor to call these into a good pharmacy that charges wholesale on vaccines (e.g. the Cure, 1025A Third Avenue, at 60th Street, Manhattan; thecureshop.com), then pick them up at the pharmacy and go to my physician who administers them for a normal insurance co-pay. David Pelavin

docs.abstract: A lifetime visitor to the seaside community shares her favorite walking trails.
docs.snippet: A lifetime visitor to the seaside community shares her favorite walking trails.
docs.lead_paragraph: DOWN a looping path deep in the Martha’s Vineyard woods, history keeps a muted vigil. It was here at Waskosim’s Rock, more than 300 years ago, that leaders of the native Wampanoag tribe met with the Mayhews (named after one of the area’s first settlers, Thomas Mayhew) to create a “Middle Line” division of property. Southwest of the boundary would remain in native control; north and east would be Mayhew territory. The great natural monument, lichen dappled and framed within a modest clearing, always surprises me when I approach it. There are no special signs along the trail. Nor will you find one of those historical markers, in cast iron, lettering raised, once you arrive. In fact, count yourself lucky to find the trailhead at all. Waskosim’s Rock, just off North Road in Chilmark, Mass., and the rest of the many splendid walking trails on Martha’s Vineyard, are a casually well-kept secret.

headline.main: Walking Martha’s Vineyard

docs.lead_paragraph: THE Halifax Seaport Farmers’ Market, in the Nova Scotian capital, is the oldest continuously running farmers’ market in North America, in operation since 1750. docs.snippet: Sean Hanratty’s pick for this week’s summer playlist is Alain Levitt, from the Chinatown restaurant Bacaro and the band, Bubbles.
docs.lead_paragraph: Where there’s a solid restaurant, a solid playlist can most likely be found. For this week’s Jam, Sean Hanratty of Santos Party House has chosen Alain Levitt, whohelps run his wife’s Venetian restaurant, Bacaro, in Manhattan’s Chinatown district. “The music is always amazing in there, and the environment and décor is incredible,” saysHanratty, who is a regular at the intimate vento Italian restaurant on Division near Ludlow. “Alain is usually behind the bar smiling and just being wonderful.” Hanratty quickly learned Levitt recently started a “super-high-energy duo, which usually involved costumes” called Bubbles. (Already, Levitt’s synth-pop outfit with the vocalist Jason Grisell has opened up for Florence and the Machine at Central Park Summerstage and played on a boat with Gang Gang Dance.) The band, who says they “just want to make everyone dance,” is hard at work on a new release. “I knew Alain’s playlist would be a super-diverse set, with songs I personally have always gravitated towards,” says Hanratty of the beat maker who hails from California. Check out Bubbles in the basement of Santos tonight.

headline.main: The Jam | Alain Levitt

docs.lead_paragraph: When ensembles that play mostly standard repertory take on contemporary works, they think of it as stretching, a broadening of their horizons. Perhaps it’s the same for a group like the International Contemporary Ensemble when it turns its attention to Mozart and, in the context of its usual wet-ink repertory, Schoenberg, as it did in a Mostly Mozart concert on Thursday evening at Alice Tully Hall. Or maybe not: however these players spend their time now, they lived and breathed the standard repertory during their student years, which were not long ago.
