docs.abstract: The biggest criticism Auto-Tune’s critics level against it is that it’s the sonic equivalent of plastic surgery or ‘roids, a digital fix that lets lousy singers skip over that whole learning-to-carry-a-tune thing (boring!) and cut straight to pop stardom’s VIP room.
docs.snippet: The biggest criticism Auto-Tune’s critics level against it is that it’s the sonic equivalent of plastic surgery or ‘roids, a digital fix that lets lousy singers skip over that whole learning-to-carry-a-tune thing (boring!) and cut straight to pop ...
docs.lead_paragraph: In the first and second installments of our guide to Auto-Tune pop — check them out here and here — we’ve tried to make the case that, when it’s used creatively, Auto-Tune can be a tool for artists, rather than a crutch. But the biggest criticism Auto-Tune’s critics level against it is that it’s the sonic equivalent of plastic surgery or ‘roids, a digital fix that lets lousy singers skip over that whole learning-to-carry-a-tune thing (boring!) and cut straight to pop stardom’s V.I.P. room. And there’s some truth to that — while the listening public’s acceptance of Auto-Tune has undeniably opened up new avenues of expression for rappers and singers, it’s also enabled some of the world’s most annoying famous people to annoy us in new ways. (Note: We mean no disrespect by including Drake here — his Auto-Tune songs are actually pretty great. But he started out as an actor, so technically he belongs in this category. Hopefully the fact that he is a rich, beautiful man will soften the blow.)

headline.main: Love Letter to Auto-Tune, Final Installment

docs.lead_paragraph: One of China’s high-speed train manufacturers, the CNR Corporation, announced Friday that it was recalling 54 of its trains from the Beijing to Shanghai route to test sensors that may be causing the trains to stop unnecessarily, such as when a passenger lights a cigarette in a restroom. docs.lead_paragraph: DeVry, the operator of DeVry University, said new undergraduate enrollment fell 26 percent, setting off a 17 percent loss in its share price. New summer enrollment dropped to 15,566, from 20,935 a year earlier, DeVry said. State and federal officials have been investigating profit-making colleges, and the Education Department has put new restrictions on financing for education companies. Adjusting to the regulations created distractions for employees, DeVry said Thursday. “Enrollment has been most impacted by the prolonged economic downturn and continued high unemployment, which has led some potential students to defer or refrain from making the commitment to enroll in college,” the company said. Stock in DeVry, which is based in Downers Grove, Ill., fell $8.90 to $44.49 a share.

docs.abstract: DEBT spirals: the term sounds ominous. As it should — these market vortexes are posing grave dangers to the global economy right now. A national debt crisis is a bank run writ large, says Kenneth Rogoff, an economics professor at Harvard and co-author with Carmen M. Reinhart of “This Time Is Different,” a history of financial crises. When a country like Greece goes deep into debt, bond investors start to worry they won’t get their money back. What can happen next is a debt spiral, a vicious circle of sinking confidence, rising borrowing costs and, ultimately, rising debt burdens. As investors lose confidence in a country, its bond prices drop, its bond yields rise and its government must pay higher interest rates to borrow. That, in turn, deepens the debt problem — and the whole thing starts over again. Debt spirals are dangerous, but they aren’t inevitable. “Country debt crises are essentially political,” Mr. Rogoff says. Governments can often stem the crisis by reducing spending, raising taxes or both. But such steps are particularly difficult — and politically unappetizing — when growth is slack, as it is now in much of the world. Tightening the belt slows growth even more, eroding tax revenue and — you guessed it — increasing the debt burden, at least in the short term. Of course, the best way to avoid a debt spiral is to avoid running up a lot of debt in the first place — when the economy is doing well. “If you walk outside without a raincoat and the sun is shining, you are fine,” Mr. Rogoff says. “But if it starts pouring, you are going to get wet.” — DYLAN LOEB McCLAIN

docs.lead_paragraph: DEBT spirals: the term sounds ominous. As it should — these market vortexes are posing grave dangers to the global economy right now. A national debt crisis is a bank run writ large, says Kenneth Rogoff, an economics professor at Harvard and co-author with Carmen M. Reinhart of “This Time Is Different,” a history of financial crises. When a country like Greece goes deep into debt, bond investors start to worry they won’t get their money back. What can happen next is a debt spiral, a vicious circle of sinking confidence, rising borrowing costs and, ultimately, rising debt burdens. As investors lose confidence in a country, its bond prices drop, its bond yields rise and its government must pay higher interest rates to borrow. That, in turn, deepens the debt problem — and the whole thing starts over again. Debt spirals are dangerous, but they aren’t inevitable. “Country debt crises are essentially political,” Mr. Rogoff says. Governments can often stem the crisis by reducing spending, raising taxes or both. But such steps are particularly difficult — and politically unappetizing — when growth is slack, as it is now in much of the world. Tightening the belt slows growth even more, eroding tax revenue and — you guessed it — increasing the debt burden, at least in the short term. Of course, the best way to avoid a debt spiral is to avoid running up a lot of debt in the first place — when the economy is doing well. “If you walk outside without a raincoat and the sun is shining, you are fine,” Mr. Rogoff says. “But if it starts pouring, you are going to get wet.” — DYLAN LOEB McCLAIN

docs.lead_paragraph: Disney’s high-profile remake of “The Lone Ranger” has ridden into the sunset, at least in its current configuration. That long-gestating movie project — starring Johnny Depp as Tonto, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer and directed by Gore Verbinski — was expected to start shooting in October in New Mexico. docs.lead_paragraph: Return to Forever IV showed off every which way on Friday night at the Beacon Theater. Otherwise the group wouldn’t have been doing its job. Jazz-rock fusion, as pioneered by previous lineups of Return to Forever in the 1970s, glorifies confrontational virtuosity. Composers show off by writing breakneck melodies, sudden meter shifts and quick-change structures; musicians show off by executing every whipsaw maneuver with pinpoint accuracy and improvising with a flourish. Done right, the music is a display of jet-fueled aerobatics; done wrong, it can be exhausting.

docs.abstract: The Union blockade of Southern ports, derided at first, had immediate consequences for Confederate civilians and soldiers alike.
docs.snippet: The Union blockade of Southern ports, derided at first, had immediate consequences for Confederate civilians and soldiers alike.
docs.lead_paragraph: Though the Union army was still getting its war footing, by August 1861 the Northern blockade of Southern ports and waterways was almost complete. That month federal ships closed the Mississippi River to commerce between loyal and secessionist states, while naval squadrons were in place off the coast of most Southern cities, from south Texas to the Chesapeake. President Lincoln had approved the blockade, known as the “Anaconda Plan,” in April. At first it was widely derided in the North and dismissed in the South—the American navy, people said, was in no shape to clamp down on thousands and thousands of miles of coastline. Nevertheless, this massive operation had an immediate impact on the Confederate economy and, as it tightened its grip on the Southern coastline, began to choke the South into submission.

headline.main: Squeezing the South into Submission

docs.abstract: The musician, artist and author Patti Smith is collaborating on a screenplay of her best-selling memoir, “Just Kids.”
docs.snippet: The musician, artist and author Patti Smith is collaborating on a screenplay of her best-selling memoir, “Just Kids.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Patti Smith is variously known as a musician, poet, artist and memoirist. Now add feature film writer to that list. She confirmed Friday that she will be collaborating with the playwright and screenwriter John Logan on an adaptation of her best-selling book “Just Kids,” which chronicled her early years in New York, focusing on her relationship with the photographer Robert Mapplethorpe. She said that she and Mr. Logan were friends and that she had particularly admired his script for “Coriolanus,” the coming film adaptation directed by a mutual friend of theirs, Ralph Fiennes. She also cited Mr. Logan’s Tony-winning play about Mark Rothko, “Red.” “It was a beautiful script and he’s very knowledgeable about art,” Ms. Smith said, speaking by phone, adding later, “He’s very knowledgeable about Robert and his work too.” There’s no director or financing set, though Ms. Smith’s literary agent, Betsy Lerner, said several producers and especially actresses have expressed interest since “Just Kids” was published last year.

headline.main: Adapting Patti Smith’s ‘Just Kids’ for the Big Screen

docs.abstract: On Going to the Sun Road in Glacier National Park, the long climb up to Logan Pass and the Continental Divide earns you a little taste of glory.
docs.snippet: On Going to the Sun Road in Glacier National Park, the long climb up to Logan Pass and the Continental Divide earns you a little taste of glory.
docs.lead_paragraph: CUT BANK, Mont. — The most direct path through Glacier National Park is called, famously and aptly, Going-to-the-Sun Road. About 51 miles long, it begins in the town of West Glacier, proceeds pleasantly along the wooded southeastern shore of Lake McDonald, providing intermittent glimpses of soaring peaks, and then, as if a giant had stepped on the end of the road, mistaking it for a seesaw, begins ruthlessly, gorgeously climbing. It goes northeast for three miles or so, then makes a hairpin turn and heads southeast along a mountain precipice and up, up, up — endlessly up if you’re on a bicycle. From the turn it’s eight miles to Logan Pass. There, at 6,646 feet, the road crosses the Continental Divide.

headline.main: Conquering the Divide

docs.lead_paragraph: One of the most important questions for small businesses hovering through all of the tumult of the last three years is whether they’ve been able to get the credit they need. The question has been hotly debated — even becoming a partisan issue last year, when Congress wrestled with the small-business lending fund that ultimately became law in the small-business jobs act. Banks tell anyone who will listen that they are eager to lend to any creditworthy business they can find. Republicans tend to put it slightly differently: small businesses that deserve credit can get it, but many are too cautious to make investments right now. Many Democrats and some small-business advocates say a good loan is hard to find.

headline.main: No Credit? No Problem

docs.lead_paragraph: The title of Josh Koenigsberg’s dark new comedy, “Herman Kline’s Midlife Crisis,” at the Beckett Theater, is a little misleading. docs.snippet: “The Submission,” the debut novel by Amy Waldman, tackles the aftermath of a terrorist attack similar to 9/11.
docs.lead_paragraph: A decade after 9/11, Amy Waldman’s nervy and absorbing new novel, “The Submission,” tackles the aftermath of such a terrorist attack head-on. The result reads as if the author had embraced Tom Wolfe’s famous call for a new social realism — for fiction writers to use their reporting skills to depict “this wild, bizarre, unpredictable, Hog-stomping baroque country of ours” — and in doing so, has come up with a story that has more verisimilitude, more political resonance and way more heart than Mr. Wolfe’s own 1987 best seller, “The Bonfire of the Vanities.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Israel has recently advanced plans for the construction of 277 housing units in the Jewish settlement of Ariel, deep inside the West Bank, the defense minister’s office said on Monday. The move, the latest in a flurry of settlement activity, comes ahead of Palestinian plans to seek United Nations recognition as a member state in the fall. Last week Israel’s Interior Ministry announced approval for a contentious 1,600-apartment complex in East Jerusalem and said it would soon approve an additional 2,700 housing units there, prompting Palestinian fury and international criticism for undermining efforts to restart peace negotiations. Israel insists on keeping Ariel under any border agreement. The Palestinians claim that territory, conquered by Israel in the 1967 war, as part of a future state.

docs.lead_paragraph: It was just this May that an article in New York magazine described AMC as “the ­fastest-­rising network in America” and wondered if that cable channel could “survive its own success.” Three months later that question seems more pressing and prophetic than ever. After rapidly building its brand of original programming around prestigious and much-lauded series like “Mad Men” and “Breaking Bad,” AMC has been roiled by behind-the-scenes disputes and controversies at every one of its signature shows – even the ones it hasn’t started broadcasting yet. Although the network received 29 Emmy Award nominations in July (including a fourth consecutive best drama nod for “Mad Men”), that moment was a rare bright spot amid months of developments that were often as gloomy as the art direction for “The Walking Dead.”

headline.main: Could Things Break Any Worse for AMC?

docs.snippet: Mr. Perry’s entry into the Republican presidential nomination could be good for publishers, if not for his competitors.
docs.lead_paragraph: The entrance of Gov. Rick Perry of Texas into the Republican presidential race may be bad news for Mitt Romney and Michele Bachmann, but so far it seems to be good news for the book business. On Tuesday, two publishers announced forthcoming books on Mr. Perry, The Associated Press reported. Metropolitan Books will publish a work, with an unprintable title, by James C. Moore, the co-author of “Bush’s Brain,” and the Texas political consultant Jason Stanford in early 2012. The book, to be subtitled “Why Rick Perry Will Make America Miss George W. Bush,” will describe Mr. Perry as an “ideologue with scant interest or success in governing,” according to the publisher’s announcement. Crown, meanwhile, said it would publish “Rick Perry and his Eggheads,” by Sasha Issenberg, as an e-book next week. The e-book, about Mr. Perry’s successful 2006 re-election campaign, is based on Mr. Issenberg’s larger work, “The Victory Lab,” which is expected in the fall of 2012 and is to explore how social science and statistical analysis are changing political campaigning.

headline.main: Two Rick Perry Books Are on the Way

docs.lead_paragraph: Handel’s opera “Orlando” has had a peculiar life. It was little more than a footnote in Handel’s day. He composed it in 1732, to an anonymous libretto based on Ariosto’s “Orlando Furioso.” He performed it only 10 times in 1733, then dropped it entirely, never bothering to revive it. It languished until the 20th century, when conductors (mostly of the period-instrument persuasion) began to nudge it into the repertory alongside “Alcina” and “Ariodante,” Handel’s two other works based on Ariosto.

With Dolce Vizio Tiramisù, which opened on Saturday, they have tapped into what appears to be a growing trend in Italy: variations on tiramisù, the traditional Venetian dessert made with a type of ladyfinger layered with a mascarpone custard and flavored with espresso and cocoa. “A tiramisù shop opened in Milan three weeks ago,” Ms. Tade said. “They beat us to it, but not by much.” Their airy shop sells tiramisù in six flavors, including lemon, berries and chocolate, with the option to assemble your own. Fabrizio Ferrari, a Michelin-starred chef from Bergamo, was in New York helping to fine-tune the recipes. docs.abstract: The berries are for sale in the Northeast.
docs.snippet: The berries are for sale in the Northeast.
docs.lead_paragraph: Small, dark, tangy wild blueberries from Maine, below left, seem to bear little relation to the typically fleshy cultivated berries, right. They are terrific in pancakes, muffins and scones. Lynn Thurston, who is a kind of blueberry broker, gets berries that farmers gather from wild bushes on their land and distributes them in the Northeast through her company, Blue Sky Produce. “It gives the farmers an alternative to selling them for the frozen market,” she said. Dry pint containers hold about two and a half cups. “That’s anywhere from 800 to 1,200 berries,” she said. “I know because I once counted them.”

docs.abstract: Suffering from decision fatigue? You may be expending your finite amount of willpower too early in the day.
docs.snippet: Suffering from decision fatigue? You may be expending your finite amount of willpower too early in the day.
docs.lead_paragraph: It may be a newly identified phenomenon among psychologists, but the symptoms seem familiar to some of the readers who have commented on my article on decision fatigue in this Sunday’s Times Magazine. docs.lead_paragraph: Not long after setting sail from Massachusetts, the Cuba-bound merchant schooner Enchantress spied a square-rigged brig approaching, painted black, with dark sails and black mastheads and yards. As the vessel drew near the merchantman, a voice ordered the Enchantress to heave to. Shortly, a boat containing an officer and six men rowed alongside. Upon climbing over the gangway, the officer confronted the merchantman’s captain, demanding immediate surrender of his vessel. Facing the muzzles of the raider’s cannon, and with only a single musket on board, the schooner’s captain had no alternative but to submit. It was piracy, plain and simple — but piracy condoned and supported by the Confederacy.

docs.lead_paragraph: Michael Lewis’s Vanity Fair article on why Germany now calls the shots in the Eurozone is delightfully, mischievously Swiftian. Lewis ties Germans’ relationship to money to, well, their relationship to excrement. As his source, he cites the work of a Berkeley anthropologist, Alan Dundes, whose book “Life Is Like a Chicken Coop Ladder” argues that German folklore is uncommonly obsessed with anality. To support the thesis that this obsession is at the root of Germany’s economic dominance (and its faulty risk-taking), Lewis uncovers myriad examples of fecal focus in German colloquialisms and proverbs.

headline.main: How German Is It?

For her part, Boucher describes her bewildering, genre-defying soundscapes and high-pitched falsetto as “post-Internet.” What, exactly, does this mean? “The music of my childhood was really diverse because I had access to everything, so the music I make is sort of schizophrenic,” she explained by phone. docs.snippet: “Conan the Barbarian,” starring Jason Momoa as the title character, delights in gore and swords.
docs.lead_paragraph: A heavy-metal fantasia scrawled in red, “Conan the Barbarian” now comes with 75 percent more gore. That’s only an estimate, though to judge by the gruesome opener that features the title character as a boy gouging enemy flesh and lopping off heads, it’s a fair guess. Having entered a forest for a newbie warrior rite of passage, baby Conan (Leo Howard) has returned to his village and its leader, his brawny, bushy father (Ron Perlman, surprise), splattered in blood and dangling several severed heads from his wee mitts. They look like grotesque puppets or maybe yo-yos, but, really, they’re just playthings for a growing barbarian.

docs.abstract: In “Class Warfare,” Steven Brill brings a sharp legal mind to the world of education reform and mounts a zealous case against America’s teachers’ unions.
docs.snippet: In “Class Warfare,” Steven Brill brings a sharp legal mind to the world of education reform and mounts a zealous case against America’s teachers’ unions.
docs.lead_paragraph: Steven Brill is a graduate of Yale Law School and the founder of Court TV, and in his new book, “Class Warfare,” he brings a sharp legal mind to the world of education reform. Like a dogged prosecutor, he mounts a zealous case against America’s teachers’ unions. From more than 200 interviews, he collects the testimony of idealistic educators, charter school founders, policy gurus, crusading school superintendents and billionaire philanthropists. Through their vivid vignettes, which he pieces together in short chapters with titles like “ ‘Colorado Says Half of You Won’t Graduate’ ” and “A Shriek on Park Avenue,” Brill conveys the epiphanies, setbacks and triumphs of a national reform movement.

headline.main: Steve Brill’s Report Card on School Reform

docs.lead_paragraph: At once familiar and gently twisted, the Australian film “Griff the Invisible” centers on a man who yearns to be a superhero. If the movie didn’t carry a 2010 date, you might think that its titular character, a hobbyist who plays at superhero, would have to spend much of his time fighting copycat charges and not villainy. In rough outline it recalls two American films, “Kick-Ass” (2010), about a teenager who wants to be a superhero and hooks up with a gun-toting girl, and “Super” (also 2010, but released last March), about a diner cook turned avenger who raises a wrench against line-cutting moviegoers and other miscreants.

docs.lead_paragraph: Paloma Josse (Garance Le Guillermic), the blasé narrator of Mona Achache’s film “The Hedgehog,” is a precociously articulate 11-year-old girl from an upper-class Parisian family who sneaks around with her father’s old camcorder as if she were a spy in her own household. Peering owl-like over her John Lennon glasses, she airily disparages her affluent “fishbowl” existence. It’s not for her, she announces. That’s why she is planning her suicide on the day she turns 12, using her mother’s pills, which she stockpiles, one at a time.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Mozart’s Sister” has just started when the French director René Féret makes the point that his fictional look at the early life and times of Wolfgang Amadeus isn’t interested in the pretty manners and nostalgia of many period movies. In truth, the film has little to do even with Wolfgang, a side note in a story focused on his only sister who’s first seen squatting on the side of a road taking care of business at a short distance from her similarly engaged father, mother and brother. This is the Family Mozart, Mr. Féret seems to declare with this scene, stripped down and at their most human.

Ms. Greig, who smiled and laughed with her lawyers before the short proceeding, pleaded not guilty to one count of conspiracy to harbor and conceal a fugitive, which carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Prosecutors said she used false identification, posed as Mr. Bulger’s wife and tried to prevent his arrest. Mr. Bulger is charged with 19 murders and other crimes. Ms. Greig’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, told reporters outside the federal court in Boston that Ms. Greig would not cooperate with the authorities and that she was an “excellent” candidate for bail.

docs.lead_paragraph: The sturgeon population in the lower Volga River — historically the world’s chief source of black caviar — has dipped by 99 percent in the past 15 years, the head of the Federal Fisheries Agency said Thursday. According to a report by the Interfax news agency, the official, Andrei Krainy, said almost all Russian sturgeon are now grown at six fisheries in the Astrakhan region in southern European Russia, where the Volga empties into the Caspian Sea. The decline began decades ago with the building of dams and with pollution that choked waterways. It has accelerated since Soviet times with organized illegal fishing and the corruption that allows it to flourish. Scientists say the surviving fish are overwhelmingly male because fishermen harvest females for their prized eggs.

headline.main: Russia: River’s Sturgeon Population Dips Drastically

docs.lead_paragraph: In the days since a Tibetan Buddhist monk in southwestern Sichuan Province set himself on fire to protest Chinese policies, the authorities have sent as many as 1,000 armed police officers to surround the monk’s monastery and have restricted telephone and Internet access, according to advocacy groups. The monk, Tsewang Norbu, was the second this year to kill himself by self-immolation. The suicide of the other monk, Phuntsog, at the Kirti Monastery, in a nearby prefecture in Sichuan, set off a violent standoff between local residents and paramilitary police, who eventually detained 300 monks. Before his suicide on Monday morning, Tsewang Norbu reportedly handed out leaflets demanding the return of the Dalai Lama, the exiled spiritual leader, and calling for an end of the repression that has intensified in the area since the clashes at Kirti Monastery.

headline.main: China: Officers Surround Monastery After Suicide

docs.lead_paragraph: A coalition opposing a law limiting rights for public employee unions rejected Gov. John Kasich’s offer to negotiate to avoid a Nov. 8 referendum, saying the measure must first be repealed. The coalition We Are Ohio, which includes labor representatives and Democrats, responded Thursday to a letter from Mr. Kasich and other Republican leaders suggesting a session to reach an agreement. A repeal “must occur prior to any meeting,” Melissa Fazekas, spokeswoman for We Are Ohio, said in a statement. The law allows 360,000 public employees to bargain only for wages, hours and work conditions. It is on hold after We Are Ohio submitted signatures to put it to a vote. The deadline to remove the issue from the ballot is Aug. 29. The Republicans’ letter said, “We are prepared to move forward immediately with legislative action to implement any agreement on changes we are able to reach together.” We Are Ohio and union groups asked Mr. Kasich and legislative leaders to call the Legislature into session to repeal the law.

headline.main: Ohio: Union Groups Reject Call to Cancel Referendum

docs.lead_paragraph: 10:59 a.m. | Updated LENOX, Mass. — It would be hard to live in America and not know some of John Williams’s music. After six decades of working in Hollywood, much of that time in collaboration with the director Steven Spielberg, he has produced an opus — 121 film scores, a symphony, a dozen concertos and other symphonic works — that would intimidate many composers. He has won five Academy Awards, four Golden Globes, five Emmys and 21 Grammys. He wrote the music for all the Star Wars and Indiana Jones movies and the first three Harry Potter films. He was the one who wrote the fearsome two-note motif from “Jaws,” and the famous five-note intergalactic message he composed for “Close Encounters of the Third Kind.” At 79, he is still going strong and recently finished scores for two more Spielberg movies, “The Adventures of Tin Tin” and “War Horse.”

docs.lead_paragraph: On Dec. 22, 1995, my husband and I received five days’ notice that our 4-month-old daughter, Sophie, was due to arrive from Korea. What better way to celebrate becoming parents for the first time than going to Union Square Cafe? But the night before Sophie’s arrival was the day after Christmas. New York was full of tourists and the Union Square Cafe was fully booked. I explained the reason for our last-minute reservation, and not only did the hostess find us a table, but when it came time for dessert, we were served a chocolate cake with “Congratulations!” written on it and a candle burning.I will always remember the graciousness of the staff and how they shared in our joy. That sense of graciousness is instilled by Meyer, and these long years later, it still comes through. NANCY ALISBERG,  West Hartford, Conn.

I, too, just navigated the waters of a breakup that involved “who will change their Facebook profile picture of us as a couple first.” The rub, however, is that I am 41 years old and divorced. I hate to break it to those kids in the (very well-meaning) conference, but nothing changes. Awkwardness, varying rules of etiquette, sexual boundaries — none of it gets all that much easier in future decades. Perhaps these teenagers will be more prepared than me and my peers for the commingling of technology and romance, for they are “digital natives.” Their ideas of privacy and even propriety are better suited for the age of online dating.

docs.lead_paragraph: One of the manifold ways our culture fails girls is in its refusal to honor or even acknowledge their deep interest in romance. docs.abstract: An account of how the Los Angeles art scene hit the big time in the 1960s.
docs.snippet: An account of how the Los Angeles art scene hit the big time in the 1960s.
docs.lead_paragraph: For contemporary art in the 1950s and ’60s, there was New York and that was it. So the old story goes. But it’s wrong. If there’s one thing that recent globally minded art history has taught us, it’s that after World War II, new art, and lots of it, was turning up in cities every­where. Los Angeles was one, and in the late ’50s, almost to its own surprise, it had a big art moment. That moment, which lasted about a decade, is the subject of “Rebels in Paradise: The Los Angeles Art Scene and the 1960s,” by Hunter Drohojowska-Philp. The book has much to recommend it: it’s fast-paced, well researched, accessibly anecdotal. But as an account of a still under­studied episode in American postwar culture, it’s oddly lopsided. It corrects one imbalance — the “only in New York” idea — but ignores ­others.

docs.abstract: Amy Waldman’s new novel concerns the controversy surrounding the choice of a Muslim to design a 9/11 memorial.
docs.snippet: Amy Waldman’s new novel concerns the controversy surrounding the choice of a Muslim to design a 9/11 memorial.
docs.lead_paragraph: When, in December 2009, The New York Times first reported plans for a Muslim community center in Lower Manhattan, there was little controversy. Only subsequently, as a result of protests organized by groups like the Freedom Defense Initiative and Stop Islamization of America, did the project become the subject of passionate debate. It was they who named the community center the “ground zero mosque.” In the months that followed, other vociferous opponents of the project emerged, among them not only conservative politicians like Newt Gingrich and some of the families of victims of 9/11, but also a number of Muslim leaders, who felt that the choice of site was insensitive and would complicate Muslim relations with the broader community. The controversy gave rise to a media frenzy that reached its height in the late summer of 2010. One imagines that the former New York Times journalist Amy Waldman heard these arguments with a combination of recognition and, perhaps, faint dismay: the general topic of her as yet unpublished first novel, “The Submission,” was proving disturbingly prescient. Her carefully imagined fiction was in the process of becoming fact.

headline.main: A Novel of Grief, Memorials and a Muslim Architect in Post-9/11 America

docs.lead_paragraph: Will you be my friend? With the possible exception of “Does this look infected?,” there is no more off-putting question. Friends are like handkerchiefs: everybody needs them, but the sight of someone asking for one is so mortifyingly vulnerable that you want to avert your eyes from the whole mess. As with handkerchiefs, it’s probably best not to look at friendship too closely, at least until you’ve had it around for a while. We stick with our friends for an entanglement of reasons, and three new picture books, while ostensibly feel-good tales about making friends, turn out to be much closer to the complicated and murky truth than one might guess from their cheery covers. docs.lead_paragraph: At a certain point in our lives something terrific happens — the stops and starts of reading begin to flow and we are able to turn our complete attention to the text itself. For many children at this stage, the familiar rules: they take particular pleasure in reading about someone in a school with routines and structures not unlike their own and enjoy meeting, in a series, their beloved characters again and again. Unconventionally designed books appeal as well — say an ersatz journal filled with just the sorts of notes and sketches the young reader could imagine making herself. Back in 1995, Marissa Moss successfully used all three of these elements in “Amelia’s Notebook.” Now, 23 books later, as her title character makes her way through middle school, she has a series for younger readers, “Daphne’s Diary of Daily Disasters.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Few creatures can compete with elephants when it comes to being both magnificent and ungainly, but human children, if we’re being honest with ourselves, come close. This sense of distant kinship, plus the fact that trunks are the coolest appendages this side of opposable thumbs, may be why elephants have been a staple of children’s literature since the days of Rudyard Kipling and Jean de Brunhoff. True, they’re not quite so numerous on the bookshelf as bunnies, mice and ducklings, but they outnumber squids by a long shot, and, what with their tree-stump legs, bulky bodies, sail-like ears and those sinuous trunks, elephants are surely more fun for illustrators to draw than just about anything, aside from explosions. So elephants: bring ’em on!

docs.snippet: “Unlikely Friendships,” No. 7 on the paperback nonfiction list, chronicles some surprising pairings from the animal kingdom. But can these relationships last long enough for a sequel?
docs.lead_paragraph: ODD COUPLES: Dog books have long been a staple of the best-seller list. But has the world ever seen as probing a work of zoological investigative reporting as “Unlikely Friendships: 47 Remarkable Stories From the Animal Kingdom”? Jennifer S. Holland’s irresistible volume, No. 7 in its sixth week on the paperback nonfiction list, features heartwarming stories of interspecies love and adorable photographs that are heart-stopping in more than one sense. Everything seems copacetic between the nearsighted deer and the black poodle shown canoodling on a bed in Canal Fulton, Ohio, but one wonders about the long-term stability of the relationship between the polar bear and the sled dog shown cavorting in the Canadian Arctic, not to mention the lioness and baby oryx shown strolling together in Kenya’s Samburu National Reserve.

headline.main: Inside the List

docs.snippet: Sean Hanratty’s pick for this week’s summer playlist is the French composer Koudlam.
docs.lead_paragraph: The French symphonic composer Koudlam is known for his otherworldly electronic beats, pulled from classical music to tribal, creating a psychedelic something from the future, maybe even space. Here he offers up this week’s playlist, which ranges from David Bowie to the relatively unknown Japanese musical cult Geinoh Yamashirogumi, headed by the scientist Tsutomu Ohashi. Sean Hanratty was introduced to Koudlam, which is French slang for “knife stab,” through the very talented visual artist Cyprien Gaillard, with whom Koudlam regularly collaborates. (Gaillard’s “Fight Club”-esque film, “Desniansky Raion,” which Koudlam scored, was coveted at the 2007 Basel Art Fair.) “I have been a huge fan of Koudlam’s for so many years,” says Hanratty of Koudlam, who is constantly traveling around the world, a hobby that no doubt influences his music. “His music has this immediate sensibility that is beautiful and detached.”

headline.main: The Jam | Koudlam

docs.lead_paragraph: As the city has worked to expand the dining options in its parks, Brooklyn Bridge Park, which is being developed along a stretch of piers on the East River, has become a lively food destination. Pier 6 at the south end, near Atlantic Avenue, has its own collection of spots — including Bark and Milk Truck, new this summer — and roof deck seating. Pier 1, at the end of Old Fulton Street, has an outpost of Ditch Plains, a cart from Calexico, Blue Marble ice cream and a wine bar. Open only through Labor Day, the concessions draw crowds of people looking to have a lobster roll, a chipotle pork taco or a glass of prosecco. Sweeping views of the harbor and the skyline are also part of the appeal. On Wednesday afternoon, the crowds included two friends discussing Ghana and microlending. DIANE CARDWELL

docs.lead_paragraph: In the past few weeks I’ve hawk-proofed my chicken yard. It’s now covered by a net, as though a trapeze artist who missed his hold might come plummeting into it. Last week, I walked out to the yard and there, in the chicken house, lay the bodies of 24 pullets. Instead of the early morning clatter of a chicken flock, silence greeted me. It was a characteristic weasel kill — all the birds dead but none removed or eaten.

docs.abstract: Jason C. Goldfarb was sentenced to three years in prison for his role in a scheme that involved a hedge fund trader and two corporate lawyers.
docs.snippet: Jason C. Goldfarb was sentenced to three years in prison for his role in a scheme that involved a hedge fund trader and two corporate lawyers.
docs.lead_paragraph: A federal judge sentenced a personal-injury lawyer, Jason C. Goldfarb, to three years in prison for his role in an insider trading scheme that involved a hedge fund trader and two corporate lawyers. Mr. Goldfarb, who worked at Brecher Fishman Pasternack Walsh Tilker & Ziegler, pleaded guilty to participating in a scheme with Zvi Goffer, a former trader at the Galleon Group, the hedge fund run by Raj Rajaratnam. He admitted to receiving tips about impending corporate mergers from Arthur Cutillo and Brien Santarlas, two low-level associates at the law firm Ropes & Gray, and then passing them to Mr. Goffer. During an April court appearance, Mr. Goldfarb, who earned college and law degrees from Villanova, said that Mr. Goffer, a friend, approached him shortly after his law school graduation and asked if he knew any corporate lawyers. Mr. Goldfarb said he eventually introduced Mr. Goffer to Mr. Cutillo, his college roommate. Both Mr. Cutillo and Mr. Santarlas have pleaded guilty to leaking information about takeovers involving 3Com and Axcan Pharma. Mr. Goffer took his case to trial and was convicted by a jury in June.

headline.main: Lawyer Sentenced in Insider Trading Case

docs.snippet: The founder of Sport Obermeyer started the business in Aspen, Colo., in the 1940s after fashioning a ski parka from a down comforter.
docs.lead_paragraph: At 91, Klaus Obermeyer remains the energetic patriarch of the family-owned skiwear company he founded in 1947. As an early ski instructor in Aspen, Colo., Obermeyer realized that his comforter stuffed with goose feathers, packed by his mother when he left Germany for North America, could provide the template for one of the first down parkas. Among Obermeyer’s other notable innovations are high-altitude sun lotion, double-paned goggles, the nylon windshirt and the dual-layer ski boot. Over the years, Sport Obermeyer has been in the forefront in developing ski gear that keeps skiers warmer, dryer, comfortable and safer on their skis. With winter inching closer, Obermeyer, an aeronautical engineer by training, is itching to get back on the slopes as he recovers from an accident last March that resulted in a broken femur in his right leg, his first serious injury in 88 years on skis. JACK BELL

docs.abstract: A variety of factors probably contributed to the movie’s opening performance, including a lack of interest by women in the subject matter and a release date when consumers were distracted with vacations or back-to-school preparations.
docs.snippet: A variety of factors probably contributed to the movie’s opening performance, including a lack of interest by women in the subject matter and a release date when consumers were distracted with vacations or back-to-school preparations.
docs.lead_paragraph: It was a weekend of carnage at the box office, but not in the way that “Conan the Barbarian” had hoped. That gory remake, financed by Nu Image for about $90 million and distributed by Lionsgate, took in an anemic $10 million in North American theaters. A variety of factors probably contributed, including a lack of interest by women in the subject matter, terrible reviews and a release date when consumers were distracted with vacations or back-to-school preparations. Two other new films also flopped. A $30 million remake of “Fright Night” (DreamWorks Studios) sold $8.3 million in tickets, while the $15 million drama “One Day” (Focus Features) took in $5 million.

headline.main: ‘Conan’ Proves Weaker Than He Looks

docs.lead_paragraph: When AMC started a division to develop original Web series, it was reasonable to expect that the online shows would resemble the channel’s ballyhooed television dramas — “Breaking Bad,” “Mad Men,” “The Walking Dead,” “The Killing” — that traffic in pitch-black humor and grim horror and film noir. The three-episode, 42-minute project, which goes live on Monday at amctv.com and Hulu, is a loving send-up of Woody Allen in his European art-house phase, complete with limited color palette, melancholy jazz score and Adam Goldberg standing in for Mr. Allen as the sex-and-maybe-love-obsessed male artist.

docs.lead_paragraph: President Felipe Calderón of Mexico has a new role in efforts to lift Mexico’s sagging tourism industry, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Calderón, 49, will appear as an adventure guide of sorts in 30-minute television programs to appear starting next month on public television stations in the United States. He wears an Indiana Jones-style hat and a harness and descends a rope into a cavern, accompanied by Peter Greenberg, host of the “The Royal Tour” series. The A.P. reports that Mr. Calderón also straps on scuba tanks to lead Mr. Greenberg into a sinkhole lake, known as a cenote, in the Yucatán and helps a Lacandon Indian paddle a boat down a jungle river. Mr. Calderón’s message is that Mexico is safe for tourists. Foreign tourism in 2010, not including border-area visitors, was down 6.3 percent from 2008 levels, and the first half of 2011 saw a 2 percent decline from the same period in 2010, according to the country’s central bank. The global economy and Mexico’s drug violence have been blamed, though foreign tourists have not been targets of the violence.

headline.main: Mexican President Stars in New Tourism Pitch

docs.snippet: A giant 4,000-year-old visitor from Egypt, Amenemhat II, seems to gaze out over the masses at the Met entry hall, and merits the room of his own that he will get in a year.
docs.lead_paragraph: A giant 4,000-year-old Egyptian visitor looms over the crowd of live humans milling antlike throughout the vast entry hall of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He is an extraordinary specimen of regal manhood. Carved from a single block of dark gray granodiorite, he sits in a form-fitting kilt on a cubic throne covered by hieroglyphics. He has the broad shoulders, narrow waist and muscular legs of a well-developed athlete. Sporting a headdress of folded striped fabric, he gazes out over the masses with imperturbable self-assurance and open eyes set in a round, youthful face. He is as thrilling as anything in the Met’s great Egyptian collection.

headline.main: A Pharaoh Lords Over a Museum

docs.abstract: LVMH executives are talking to Marc Jacobs about moving from Louis Vuitton to Dior, as Women’s Wear Daily reported Monday.
docs.snippet: LVMH executives are talking to Marc Jacobs about moving from Louis Vuitton to Dior, as Women’s Wear Daily reported Monday.
docs.lead_paragraph: I am not at all surprised that LVMH executives are talking to Marc Jacobs about moving from Louis Vuitton to Dior, as Women’s Wear Daily reported on Monday. Not to disparage Mr. Jacobs’s talents, but where else can they look? With few exceptions, the strategy of Bernard Arnault, the chairman of LVMH, has been to load up his brands with big, bankable stars, and there are not many of them available. Shortly after John Galliano was dismissed from Dior, editors put together an imaginary list of candidates: Alber Elbaz of Lanvin, Tom Ford, Nicolas Ghesquiere of Balenciaga, among others. Yet for obvious reasons these individuals might be happy where they are, as would Sarah Burton, the creative director of Alexander McQueen, whose name surfaced soon after the royal wedding in April. According to WWD, she rebuffed overtures from LVMH.

headline.main: New Names in the Dior Hat

docs.lead_paragraph: Politicians who promise transparency could learn something from the singer Susana Baca, who is now the Peruvian minister of culture. She is completing an extensive tour planned before her appointment in July. At City Winery on Sunday night, her music was as open as can be: a tidy, lightly propulsive mesh of largely acoustic instruments (the upright bass was electric) that never obscured her gentle but drily resolute voice. And in that show of clarity was a graceful bundle of agendas: memory and modernization, mourning and celebration. Dressed in white, Ms. Baca beamed through her set, sometimes with eyes closed as if she were entranced; now and then she let the rhythms carry her into dance steps.

headline.main: It’s Not Every Cabinet Minister Who Can Also Take to the Stage

docs.lead_paragraph: Representative Jason Chaffetz, Republican of Utah, announced Monday that he would not run for the Senate, removing a potentially formidable rival to Senator Orrin Hatch as he seeks a seventh term. Mr. Chaffetz, a Tea Party favorite, had signaled that he was ready to take on Mr. Hatch in the party’s nominating process, and he was given a reasonable chance of success after Utah Republicans decided in 2010 to oust Robert F. Bennett, an 18-year veteran of the Senate, in favor of a newcomer, Mike Lee. But Mr. Chaffetz said he would instead seek re-election to the House to focus on a push for fiscal discipline. “I can spend the next 15 months doing my job, or I can spend the next 15 months campaigning to do Senator Hatch’s,” he said in a statement. “Despite being tempted to compete for the privilege of serving in the U.S. Senate — and being convinced I could win — I won’t allow a fight for that seat to distract me from what I was sent to Washington to do.”

headline.main: Tea Party Favorite Won’t Challenge Senate Republican

docs.snippet: Daphne Rubin-Vega (“Rent”) will play Stella and Wood Harris (“The Wire”) will play Mitch in a coming Broadway production that will star Blair Underwood as Stanley and Nicole Ari Parker as Blanche DuBois.
docs.lead_paragraph: They’ve played some of the toughest characters that New York and Baltimore had to offer, and now Daphne Rubin-Vega and Wood Harris are headed into a famously rugged depiction of New Orleans in a 2012 Broadway production of “A Streetcar Named Desire,” its producers said on Tuesday. Ms. Rubin-Vega, who originated the role of Mimi in the New York Theater Workshop and Broadway incarnations of “Rent,” will play Stella, the timid wife of Stanley and sister of Blanche DuBois. Mr. Harris, who played the drug kingpin Avon Barksdale on the HBO drama “The Wire,” will play Mitch, Stanley’s muscle-building pal who develops an attraction to Blanche. Blair Underwood and Nicole Ari Parker were previously announced to play Stanley and Blanche in this latest “Streetcar” revival, the first time that the Tennessee Williams play has been presented on Broadway since 2005. It will be directed by Emily Mann, the artistic director of the McCarter Theater in Princeton, N.J., and presented in the spring at a theater to be determined. It is produced by Stephen Byrd and Alia M. Jones of Front Row Productions, who produced the 2008 Broadway revival of “Cat on a Hot Tin Roof” that featured an African-American cast.

headline.main: Daphne Rubin-Vega and Wood Harris Set for ‘Streetcar’ Revival on Broadway

docs.snippet: The actress-turned-director takes hold of her career as a storyteller in her directorial debut, “Higher Ground.”
docs.lead_paragraph: For Vera Farmiga, a Ukrainian-American actress whose reputably selective film career includes “Down to the Bone,” “The Departed” and 2009’s “Up in the Air,” which garnered her an Academy Award nomination, the movies are a family affair. In her directorial debut, “Higher Ground,” based on the novel by Carolyn S. Briggs and opening on Aug. 26, Farmiga handles a solid cast of actors, which includes her younger sister Taissa Farmiga and John Hawkes (“American Gangster” and the forthcoming drama “Martha Marcy May Marlene”), as she recounts the story of a woman named Corinne Walker — a mother and wife and child of God — who struggles with doubt and disbelief as she searches for her identity, her “instrument.” “I wanted to make sure that what pervaded the film was the character of music and its capacity to unite people,” says Farmiga of her hymn-heavy picture, produced by Farmiga and her rocker husband, Renn Hawkey, of the band Deadsy. Just days before the film’s opening, Farmiga spoke to The Moment about family, how she came upon “Higher Ground” and what separates the girls from the women.

headline.main: Asked & Answered | Vera Farmiga

docs.lead_paragraph: The Blind Barber in the East Village loves a good surprise. On the surface it operates as a classic barbershop, piles of shorn hair on the floor and all, but it also houses a secret speakeasy in the back room offering banquette seating, live D.J.’s and top-shelf whiskey. Now, not even their canisters of barbicide can be trusted. Teaming up with Joya, the New York company that makes all-natural fragrances for Rodarte and Opening Ceremony, the Bind Barber has crafted a signature soy wax candle that’s packaged to look just like the antiseptic used to keep combs and scissors minty fresh. docs.lead_paragraph: With a title like “American Ninja Warrior,” one can’t help but raise an intrigued eyebrow, and that curiosity turned into solid ratings for NBC on Monday when the season finale of the obstacle course program reached nearly four million total viewers. Its audience actually grew in the second hour, averaging 4.3 million viewers and winning the 10 p.m. time slot in the 18-to-49-year-old demographic. docs.lead_paragraph: Rafael Nadal was working his way into a point about tennis rivalries. It was near the end of the third day of the Wimbledon Championships in late June, and Nadal, an hour or so earlier, efficiently dispensed with his second-round opponent, the hard-hitting but chronically inconsistent American Ryan Sweeting, in straight sets. Now, freshly showered, his longish hair going its own way, his biceps stretching the sleeves of his tight-fitting polo shirt, Nadal, at that moment the No. 1 men’s tennis player in the world, was seated behind a table in a small auditorium at Wimbledon’s press center, weighing what to say. He looked down, toyed a bit with the bottle of water in front of him, brought his hands together, slowly lifted his head and tilted it, then began a smile but shut it down as he looked at me.

docs.lead_paragraph: You could tell almost right away that the earthquake that rattled New York on Tuesday was not really a big deal. If it had seriously disrupted the rhythms of the city, don’t you think the mayor would have urged people to do something like take in a Broadway show?That, you surely recall, was his tin-eared recommendation in December when much of the city was brought to a standstill by the Great Blizzard of 2010 and many New Yorkers couldn’t dig their way out of their own streets, let alone make it to the theater. So the absence of any such suggestion this time was reassuring, a clear signal that we would be all right.

headline.main: Unflappable, but a Little Shaken

docs.lead_paragraph: “Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit” is probably the most popular sentence in the world that is not meant to be read. “Lorem Ipsum” (shorthand for the entire, seemingly endless body of Latin text) is the green screen of the publishing world — placeholder copy used by designers to replicate how a block of text will look and how many words it will fit before swapping in the fully written article. docs.abstract: Whatever comes next, the fall of Qaddafi is very good news.
docs.snippet: Whatever comes next, the fall of Qaddafi is very good news.
docs.lead_paragraph: For months, almost every development out of Libya seemed to confirm my initial pessimism about our quasi-war against Muammar Qaddafi. But happily that’s changed in the last week, with the sudden collapse of his regime and the apparent victory of the rebels. As in post-Saddam Iraq and post-Taliban Afghanistan, many of the scenarios for what comes next in Libya could ultimately pose as many risks to American interests as Qaddafi himself ever did, and I agree with all the voices pointing out that the tyrant’s fall doesn’t necessarily vindicate our intervention, to say nothing of the dubiously legal means by which America was taken to war in North Africa. But I also think it’s important for critics of the war to acknowledge the significance of the last few days’ events. While few intervention skeptics “maintained that we could not possibly defeat the regime” (as Ramesh Ponnuru puts it), many of us worried that the administration’s (understandably) risk-averse approach to the conflict might create a permanent stalemate, leaving an armed-and-dangerous Qaddafi in power in Tripoli while Western warplanes circled impotently overhead. Qaddafi’s defeat doesn’t necessarily promise a happy outcome in the long run, but at the very least it guarantees that we will be spared that particular worst-case scenario, while holding out the possibility of a Libya unified and at peace — rather than a Libya partitioned and perpetually patrolled by Western forces, which is where we seemed to be headed a month ago. Declarations of victory are ridiculously premature, but for a country and a White House starved for any sort of good news, the fall of Qaddafi should be cause for (suitably restrained) celebration.

headline.main: Libya: The End and the Beginning

She went on to guide and train young dancers for nearly four decades, including Robert Battle, the company’s new artistic director. docs.lead_paragraph: You can drive almost anywhere in the state of Michigan — pick a point at random and start moving — and you will soon come upon the wreckage of American industry. If you happen to be driving on the outer edge of Midland, you’ll also come upon a cavern of steel beams and ductwork, 400,000 square feet in all. When this plant, which is being constructed by Dow Kokam, a new venture partly owned by Dow Chemical, is up and running early next year, it will produce hundreds of thousands of advanced lithium-ion battery cells for hybrid and electric cars. docs.lead_paragraph: All was froth and pitch at Iceage’s sold-out show on Monday night at the Mercury Lounge, and this felt almost clinically prescribed. Elias Bender Ronnenfelt, the band’s vocalist, stalked the tight stage with sulky agitation, shoulders hunched, barking into his fist. Behind him drums and bass pumped in machinelike overdrive amid a gnarl of distorted guitar. Before him, the crowd swayed in heaves, half soaked with spilled beer. Scheduled to go on at 11:30, the band had started precisely on time.

docs.lead_paragraph: Casa Midy’s Montelargo banquette ($1,250), like many of the company’s pieces, is an amalgam of French and Mexican references reflecting the owners’ backgrounds. Anne-Marie Midy is French, and the banquette’s silhouette is inspired by park benches from that country, while Jorge Almada’s Mexican heritage is evident in the way the saddle leather is affixed to the frame, with belts and tassels. “My dad was an amateur bullfighter, and would wear leather chaps called zahones that are fastened with straps to the body,” Mr. Almada said. “The idea was to fasten the leather panel to the frame in the same manner.” Information, in Mexico: 011-52-415-15-2-04-03 or casamidy.com.

docs.abstract: This Sunday, the Museum of Art and Design transforms into a vortex of cyberpunk phosphorescence.
docs.snippet: This Sunday, the Museum of Art and Design transforms into a vortex of cyberpunk phosphorescence.
docs.lead_paragraph: This Sunday, the seventh floor of the Museum of Art and Design will be transformed into a 1990s vortex of cyberpunk phosphorescence, Web 1.0 social networking and conceptual snacking (e.g., scented high-potency oxygen). Snack the Planet kicks off the museum’s Fun fellowship, which gives local night-life innovators carte blanche to create outsize party experiences at the museum. Lauren Devine and Patrik Sandberg, who masterminded the event, were inspired by the seminal Angelina Jolie film “Hackers” (1995) and its credo to “hack the planet,” but promise to collude with the present as well, with performances by the up-and-coming acts Pictureplane, Teengirl Fantasy and Mykki Blanco; an immersive multimedia “entertainment zone” designed by Thunder Horse Video; and advanced tweeting modalities engineered by DIS Magazine’s Nick Scholl, whose colleagues are supplying the souvenir branded condoms. Next up, Gag!, the long-running night at Metropolitan gay bar in Williamsburg, Brooklyn hosted by Cameron Cooper and Zach Cole, will host what it is billing as a free store (in fact it will operate on a barter system) specializing in homegrown hipster esoterica during Fashion Week.Snack the Planet: Saturday, Aug. 27, 12-5 p.m. and Sunday, Aug. 28, 12-10 p.m. Bands play on Sunday only, starting at 5 p.m.

headline.main: Let the Fun Begin

docs.abstract: Long noted for its bike culture and all things independent and artisan, in recent years the city has emerged as the capital of West Coast urban cool.
docs.snippet: Long noted for its bike culture and all things independent and artisan, in recent years the city has emerged as the capital of West Coast urban cool.
docs.lead_paragraph: WITH its celebrated bike culture and obsession with all things independent and artisan, Portland is a small-scale metropolis with an outsize cultural footprint. Spread across the twin banks of the Willamette River, this provincial hub of the Pacific Northwest has more than its share of natural beauty and an earnest, outdoorsy reputation. But in recent years, the city has emerged as the capital of West Coast urban cool, earning it a television series, IFC’s “Portlandia,” devoted to satirizing its aesthetic and progressive social bent. Indeed, Portland — whose nicknames include Beervana and Soccer City, USA — is easy to poke fun at. It’s also hard to resist.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Portland, Ore.

docs.snippet: Delicious destinations for tea and its accompaniments can be found in some of the chicest corners of Paris.
docs.lead_paragraph: Megumi Ibusuki poured the cool liquid from an iron pot into a squat glass. She placed it, gently, on a square of striped raw silk set in a dark wood square tray. She urged me to sniff the aroma and observe the liquid’s color before I brought the glass to my lips. The liquid — the palest celadon — tasted like, well, Mount Fuji evanescence. I was sitting in a boutique on one of the chicest corners of Paris’s Sixth Arrondissement, at the bottom of the rue de Seine, across the street from Gérard Mulot, the luxury traiteur. But spiritually, I was in Japan.

headline.main: Lumière | All the Tea in Paris

docs.abstract: The 10th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks is inspiring a host of events in almost every genre.
docs.snippet: The 10th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks is inspiring a host of events in almost every genre.
docs.lead_paragraph: SAMUEL Beckett might have been right about the fundamental tension between human frailty and the expressive instinct of human culture. “If you really get down to the disaster,” he once observed, “the slightest eloquence becomes unbearable.” But it has never kept humans from seeking refuge in art and turning to it to try to comprehend tragedy. And in the coming days and weeks surrounding the 10th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, the outpouring of music, film, visual art, theater, books and public forums revisiting the events and the victims of that Tuesday morning will be not only immense but also powerful and richly diverse.

headline.main: Artists Rise to an Occasion for Reflection
headline.print_headline: Artists Rise To an Occasion For Reflection

docs.abstract: Vera Farmiga stars in this film, her directorial debut, a drama that weighs the merits of faith against a secular sensibility.
docs.snippet: Vera Farmiga stars in this film, her directorial debut, a drama that weighs the merits of faith against a secular sensibility.
docs.lead_paragraph: There is something remarkable — you might even say miraculous — about the way “Higher Ground” makes its gentle, thoughtful way across the burned-over terrain of the American culture wars. The film, directed with disarming grace and sharp intelligence by Vera Farmiga (who also stars in it), is about the conflict between skepticism and religious faith, but it does not treat that battle as an either/or, winner-take-all proposition. Movies about belief and believers frequently succumb to woozy piety or brittle contempt, but “Higher Ground” belongs, along with Robert Duvall’s “Apostle” and Michael Tolkin’s underappreciated “Rapture,” among the elect. Focused with sympathetic intensity on the ordeal of a single soul, it illuminates, as though from within, a complex spiritual struggle.

headline.main: Navigating Between Faith and Skepticism

docs.snippet: “Tales,” overseen by Cristian Mungiu, is a hearty satirical guffaw of gallows humor that illustrates how laughter helped buoy the spirits of an oppressed citizenry.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s only a matter of degree. The absurdities of “Tales From the Golden Age,” a facetiously titled anthology of six “urban legends” of Romanian life in the waning days of the Ceausescu dictatorship, aren’t that much crazier than everyday existence anywhere else in our paranoid world. Consider that in a typical episode of “The Office” you will find a gentler, miniature version of the same kind of dissembling, bureaucratic idiocy and hierarchical kowtowing. The difference, of course, is that the employees of the Dunder Mifflin Paper Company of Scranton, Pa., don’t risk prison or worse after inadvertently offending a higher-up.

docs.lead_paragraph: On Dec. 11, 2008, Bernard L. Madoff confessed to F.B.I. agents that he was running an immense Ponzi scheme, involving tens of billions of dollars from investors all around the world. That might have been a day of triumph for Harry Markopolos, the whistle-blower who for years had tried to get the Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as several business publications, to investigate Mr. Madoff’s activities. Instead, the arrest provided only momentary relief. As set out in the documentary “Chasing Madoff,” Mr. Markopolos panicked, thinking it would be only a matter of time before embarrassed S.E.C. agents would break into his home in Whitman, Mass., seeking to erase his records of their incompetence. Of course, as with everything else in this case, the S.E.C. did nothing.

docs.abstract: “Follies” reminiscences from theater folks who have seen productions of the show from the original 1971 and beyond.
docs.snippet: “Follies” reminiscences from theater folks who have seen productions of the show from the original 1971 and beyond.
docs.lead_paragraph: EVERY Broadway musical has its originalists, the devotees who judge every subsequent production against the memory of the first one. The you-had-to-be-there contingent is particularly strong for “Follies,” Stephen Sondheim and James Goldman’s 1971 collaboration with the directors Harold Prince and Michael Bennett. Goldman’s book and Mr. Sondheim’s music and lyrics use the reunion of showgirls from a fictitious Ziegfeld Follies-style revue to juxtapose the dazzling heyday of Depression-era Broadway with the decades of ambivalence and regret that followed. The latest revival — directed by Eric Schaeffer and featuring Bernadette Peters, Jan Maxwell, Ron Raines and Danny Burstein — will undoubtedly generate its own share of memories when it opens on Sept. 12 at the Marquis Theater. Until then here are a handful of “Follies” reminiscences from people who have seen ’em all (but particularly the original one) and are still here.

headline.main: Memories of Great Gams of the Past

docs.snippet: Steven Soderbergh’s latest film, “Contagion,” has an all-star cast and a sky-high body count and belongs to the fitfully popular Hollywood genre of the disaster movie.
docs.lead_paragraph: The new thriller “Contagion” revisits a conundrum that has bedeviled many filmmakers over the years: how do you make a movie about a virus, a villain that isn’t even visible? Epidemic movies have sidestepped the problem by focusing on the aftermath of a deadly plague, as with “The Omega Man” (1971) and “12 Monkeys” (1995), both set in postapocalyptic wastelands. Another option is to invent a disease with outlandish symptoms, as in “The Crazies” (1973), in which the infected turn homicidally insane, or “28 Days Later” (2002), in which they become zombies.

headline.main: A Virus Movie Determined to Get Real

docs.abstract: Old World design meets retail in Fresh’s newly redesigned store on Broadway.
docs.snippet: Old World design meets retail in Fresh’s newly redesigned store on Broadway.
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s nothing stale about Fresh’s new retail concept. The beauty brand’s fragrant flagship in Manhattan’s Union Square has been completely redesigned by Mapos, a young architecture firm headed up by two former Peter Marino disciples. Inspired by Old World bakeries, laboratories and apothecaries, the space is bisected by a massive reclaimed walnut “kitchen” table that contains stacks of vintage botanical books and offers a comfy place to perch while testing products. Custom and antique details abound, including an old English communal wash basin, a unique “Sensorial Bar,” (where discontinued fragrances are available on tap) and a large glass display case that makes Fresh’s prettily packaged soaps look like confections in a pastry shop.

docs.snippet: A mother-daughter car trip along Lake Michigan’s eastern shores, stopping at beach towns along the way.
docs.lead_paragraph: I KNEW my mission was achieved when my oldest daughter sailed past me on her stomach, shouting, “It’s like an ocean without saltwater!” Her sister was close behind, riding another wave. Though I spent my childhood summers boating and swimming in Lake Michigan, my two teenage daughters, Harriet, 19, and Florence, 15, had never known the joys of plunging into the clear, cool, open waters of a Great Lake. Therefore, it seemed only fitting that our mother-daughter trip last month should be to my old stomping, or rather swimming, grounds. Rather than take a nostalgic trip to the top of Michigan’s mitten, I decided we should instead hit what would be virgin territory for me as well and head to the west coast, where I had heard that a half-dozen beach towns could easily be visited in a four-day period, thanks to 170 miles of gentle lakeside highway.

headline.main: Memory-Making on Michigan’s Beaches

docs.lead_paragraph: Baseball is a sunshine sport, in essence a daytime game whenever it’s played, but there is something of the night about it: a darkness that resonates in the deepest part of the American psyche. For the batter, of course, it’s a game defined by failure most of time, but on a grander scale too our national pastime often seems free of what William James called our “national disease”: the “exclusive worship of the bitch-goddess success.” Failure gives baseball its pleasing, melancholic tang; the boys of summer are always in ruin, after all, and the dirge of the Cubs forever drowns out the anthem of the Yankees. It seems somehow fitting that one of the worst diseases imaginable is named after one of the greatest baseball players. “It breaks your heart,” the former president of Yale and commissioner of Major League Baseball A. Bartlett Giamatti said of the game. “It is designed to break your heart.”

docs.snippet: A biography and a memoir examine the life and career of the author of “Catch-22.”
docs.lead_paragraph: “Oh God, this is a calamity for American literature,” Kurt Vonnegut said on learning of Joseph Heller’s death in 1999. John Updike was less alarmed: Heller “wasn’t top of the chart” as a writer, he reflected, though he was “a sweet man” and his first novel, “Catch-22” was “important.” Note the Updikean judiciousness of “important”: he didn’t say he liked the book, but it was a great cultural bellwether as novels go, and it has endured. Despite mixed reviews on publication in 1961, “Catch-22” was soon adopted by college students who recognized a kindred spirit in Yossarian, the bombardier who rebels against a materialistic bureaucracy hellbent on killing him. “Better Yossarian than Rotarian” became a popular slogan, all the more so with the timely (for the novel’s sake) military escalation in Vietnam, which became the “real” subject of “Catch-22” and partly accounts for its sales of more than 10 million copies to date. It’s hard to argue with that kind of importance.

docs.lead_paragraph: Enrique Krauze is a well-known historian in Mexico. He is also a documentary filmmaker and television talking head renowned for his mellifluous basso voice, a publisher of elegant coffee-table books and a canny operator within the upper murks of Mexican politics. He is the editor of a glossy highbrow magazine called Letras Libres. There are corners of the Spanish-speaking universe in which he is omnipresent, and even a few corners of the English-speaking universe in which his byline is hard to miss. I have been following his work for decades. I subscribe to his magazine. Occasionally I contribute to it. He has always seemed to me a keen and judicious political observer, worldly and instinctively liberal. But now it occurs to me that he is also marked by a rare and attractive gift for noticing the several ways that, under the bright sun of the imagination, the kingdom of politics and the kingdom of literature sometimes merge.

docs.lead_paragraph: In the Japanese art of sumi-e, strokes of ink are brushed across sheets of rice paper, the play of light and dark capturing not just images but sensations, not just surfaces but the essence of what lies within. Simplicity of line is prized, extraneous detail discouraged. Although Julie Otsuka was born and raised in California and trained as a painter in the Western tradition, she seems perfectly attuned to the spirit of sumi-e. Otsuka claims to have been a failure as an artist, but she might only have erred in choosing the wrong medium. Proof arrived almost a decade ago, long after she’d traded painting for writing, with the publication of her first novel, “When the Emperor Was Divine,” a spare but resonant portrait of one Japanese-­American family’s daily life, at home and in the internment camps, during World War II. Now she returns with a second novel, also employing a minimalist technique, that manages to be equally intimate yet much more expansive.

docs.lead_paragraph: I won’t blame you for not believing this: The photograph on the cover of Tracy K. Smith’s “Life on Mars” is the same one I see every day on my computer desktop. It’s a dramatic and vivid picture from the Hubble Space Telescope, with colors I imagine J. M. W. Turner would have admired, of the Cone Nebula, a pillar of dust and gas some 2,500 light-years from Earth. Scientists say it’s an incubator for baby stars. I’ve long used the image as an efficient and emphatic corrective for solipsism. I look at it when I find myself fretting about, say, book review deadlines or my spotty gym attendance. You can’t simultaneously contemplate the vastness of the universe and take such problems seriously.

Our so-called advances have backfired, transporting us to a medieval perdition, rendering us cannibalistic and crazed. Progress — often a bugaboo called capitalism, as in Jack London’s novel “The Iron Heel” — eradicates good sense and civility, while violence is endemic in every town.

docs.snippet: On Canada’s Prince Edward Island, all roads lead to tasty seafood.
docs.lead_paragraph: We came, we shucked, we concurred with the “Gentle Island” tag line. Prince Edward Island, a crescent-shaped patch of land off the coast of New Brunswick, and Canada’s smallest province, is the kind of place where the dinner rush starts at 4:30. During the high season, which runs from May to October, it’s one big seafood banquet: oysters, clams, mussels, halibut, lobsters, haddock, salmon and scallops are all on the menu, and all from just down the road. The seafood used to hit your plate deep fried beyond recognition, but these days your fish could come grilled, your steamers actually steamed. Last month, my husband, our 1-year-old son and I set off in search of fishy stuff and found plenty, along with a few other simple summer pleasures, like the local classic-rock radio station (hello, Queen!).

Martin has decided to abandon his “Song of Ice and Fire” series and take up extreme knitting instead. Rather, it’s a profanity-laced memoir-cum-manifesto from the magician and outspoken atheist Penn Jillette, the taller and louder half of Penn & Teller. The book is structured around Jillette’s alternatives to the Ten Commandments (take the Lord’s name in vain all you want, but be sure to “say what you mean, even when talking to yourself”), but we also get reminiscences about his moderately Congregationalist childhood in Massachusetts, his conflicted admiration for Siegfried and Roy, and the “atheist baptisms” held at his Las Vegas home, the Slammer, which tend to involve lots of bacon, “nude cornstarch wrestling” and a fat Elvis impersonator. We also learn some good post-show lobby pickup lines: he laughed hardest at the woman who asked, “Is your name Debbie?” but married the one who started talking about Richard Dawkins. As for their children, his wife may be Jewish (or, as he puts it, a nonbeliever whose forebears happened to be Jewish), but “they are atheist and their culture is Vegas — and even that’s too much tribalism for me.”

docs.abstract: Sean Hanratty’s pick for this week’s summer playlist is the timeless Marianne Faithfull.
docs.snippet: Sean Hanratty’s pick for this week’s summer playlist is the timeless Marianne Faithfull.
docs.lead_paragraph: The legendary English singer-songwriter Marianne Faithfull, who is also an actress, presents us with her playlist this week. “It’s heavy in the cornerstone classics of music,” says the Jam‘s curator, Sean Hanratty, of the list, which includes Leonard Cohen and the Clash. “It’s full of the timeless stuff that you never really lose, the records you own and would never part with.” Faithfull’s first hit, “As Tears Go By” (1964), which Mick Jagger, Keith Richards and the Rolling Stones manager Andrew Loog Oldham helped write, remains one of the best ballads of all time. The song, along with her highly publicized relationship with Jagger, put her on the map as one of rock’s biggest stars. “You Can’t Always Get What You Want,” on the Stones album “Let It Bleed,” released in 1969, was one of many songs written about Faithfull. “I think some people forget — certainly not me — that she also co-wrote ‘Sister Morphine,’ ” says Hanratty of the track on the Stones’s 1971 “Sticky Fingers” album. (The song is reportedly about her life and battles with drug abuse, specifically heroin.) For the past five decades, we have seen Faithfull reinvent herself as a performer and musician, in collaborations with the likes of David Bowie, Tom Waits, Emmylou Harris, Nick Cave and others, while keeping her place as one of the most influential female singer-songwriters of all time. “With the impending hurricane and Virginia’s earthquake, we are kind of in need of the classics,” Hanratty says. Faithfull will perform her classics, as well as songs from this year’s album, “Horses and High Heels,” at Manhattan’s City Winery on Dec. 18.

headline.main: The Jam | Marianne Faithfull

docs.lead_paragraph: The government has approved plans for a $30 billion public works project dubbed “Le Grand Paris,” which President Nicolas Sarkozy hopes will prove a durable legacy of his leadership. The project, whose approval was noted in an official decree published Friday, will include the construction of more than 100 miles of automatic subway lines and 57 new stations, linking the suburbs around Paris in a massive figure 8. Mr. Sarkozy had aspired to remake the capital and solicited proposals from renowned architects, who offered extravagant visions of airborne parks, expansive greenery and futuristic towers. But his ambitions ran up against political and financial limits. The first new subways are planned to be in operation by 2018, according to the Société du Grand Paris, the state authority in charge of the project.

docs.abstract: The maker of tobacco products lost a bid for a new trial in its decade-long effort to extract patent royalties from Reynolds American on a way to reduce carcinogens in cigarettes.
docs.snippet: The maker of tobacco products lost a bid for a new trial in its decade-long effort to extract patent royalties from Reynolds American on a way to reduce carcinogens in cigarettes.
docs.lead_paragraph: Star Scientific, a maker of tobacco products, lost a bid for a new trial in its decade-long effort to extract patent royalties from Reynolds American on a way to reduce carcinogens in cigarettes. Losing the bid set off a 40 percent decline in its share price Friday. While the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in Washington today upheld the validity of two Star patents, the panel said there was no need to retry the infringement case against Reynolds that Star lost in 2009. Judge Randall Rader said in the 2-to-1 opinion that a new trial would not change the outcome as “there was substantial untainted evidence before the jury to support a verdict of noninfringement.” The patents cover a curing process that prevents “bacterial activity” in tobacco leaves, resulting in the lowest levels of cancer-causing nitrosamines, according to Star. Stock in the company, which is based in Glen Allen, Va., fell $1.19, or nearly 40 percent, to $1.81 a share.

headline.main: Star Scientific Loses Bid for Patent Royalties
headline.print_headline: Star Scientific Loses Bid for Patent Royalties
