docs.snippet: These days, a version of the parties held in the early days of the Bauhaus school, called Farbfest, held in Dessau, about an hour and a half outside of Berlin, are back. This year’s festivities will be on Sept. 2 and 3.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the decade or so before the Nazis came to power in Germany, the Bauhaus school was known for its groundbreaking modern art, architecture and design — and its terrific parties. In fact, Walter Gropius, the Bauhaus founder, decreed that wild theme parties — where students and professors would dress up, recite poetry, show what they were working on, and generally have a good time — were to be part of the curriculum. These days, a version of those parties, called Farbfest, held at the Bauhaus building in Dessau, about an hour and a half outside of Berlin, are back. This year’s festivities will be on Sept. 2 and 3.

headline.main: Outside of Berlin, Bauhaus-Themed Fun

docs.abstract: Hurricane Irene has claimed a performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony scheduled for Sunday afternoon at the Tanglewood Festival in Lenox, Mass.
docs.snippet: Hurricane Irene has claimed a performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony scheduled for Sunday afternoon at the Tanglewood Festival in Lenox, Mass.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Boston Symphony Orchestra has canceled its performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony scheduled for Sunday afternoon at the Tanglewood Festival in Lenox, Mass., because of the approach of Hurricane Irene. The performance of the Ninth Symphony, which traditionally ends the orchestra’s season at the festival, was to have been conducted by Lorin Maazel. All other Tanglewood events scheduled for Sunday have also been canceled, but the Tanglewood Jazz Festival is still scheduled to run from Thursday to next Sunday. The orchestra says that this is the first time it has canceled a concert in its 75-year residence at Tanglewood, despite occasionally heavy weather in the surrounding Berkshire Hills. Refunds will be available. Information can be found online or, as of Monday, at (617) 638-9395.

headline.main: Boston Symphony Orchestra Performance Is Canceled

docs.lead_paragraph: Vania King, Sania Mirza and Aisam-ul-Haq Qureshi, three of the best doubles players in the world, participated in a roundtable discussion about tennis and culture on Friday in front of more than 50 New York Times staffers. King, 22, a Taiwanese-American from Monterey Park, Calif., and Boynton Beach, Fla., is the defending doubles champion at the United States Open and winner of the Wimbledon doubles title in 2010. Qureshi, 31, of Lahore, Pakistan, reached the doubles finals of the U.S. Open last year, where he and Rohan Bopanna, of India, lost to Bob and Mike Bryan in two tiebreakers. Mirza, 24, who was born in Mumbai, India, and currently lives in Dubai, was a doubles finalist at the French Open this year.

headline.main: Doubles Standouts Talk About Culture and Collaboration

docs.abstract: The modern world began — and ended — with visions of an ideal state.
docs.snippet: The modern world began — and ended — with visions of an ideal state.
docs.lead_paragraph: The modern world was inaugurated by two books with opposing perspectives, published at the same time in the early years of the 16th century: Machiavelli’s “The Prince” and Thomas More’s “Utopia.” Modernity came to a close with the collapse of all those attempts, both collective and liberal, that had been made to bring utopia about in history. Here I should like to reflect on that beginning and that end, insofar as they involve the status of utopia.

headline.main: The Meaning of Utopia

docs.snippet: Los Angeles County Superior Court disclosed in a statement that Mel Gibson and his ex-girlfriend Oksana Grigorieva had reached an agreement resolving the many issues between them.
docs.lead_paragraph: Whatever the peace settlement contains, the fight is over. At an unusually late hour — after 8 p.m. on Friday — Los Angeles County Superior Court disclosed in a statement that Mel Gibson and his ex-girlfriend Oksana Grigorieva had reached an agreement resolving the many issues between them. They had been engaged in an epic court battle over custody of their young daughter, and related financial matters. The fight involved claims of abuse by Mr. Gibson and of extortion by Ms. Grigorieva. But the court said there is a deal between the two, the terms of which will be reviewed at a hearing scheduled for 8:30 a.m. Wednesday in the courtroom of Judge Peter D. Lichtman. The court hears custody issues behind closed doors. But issues concerning the financial agreement between Mr. Gibson and Ms. Grigorieva will be reviewed in an open hearing, the court’s statement said.

headline.main: Mel Gibson Settles With Former Girlfriend

docs.lead_paragraph: Jonas Kaufmann, a major international tenor who has become an increasingly important presence at the Metropolitan Opera, plans to go ahead with an Oct. 30 recital at the house just two months after undergoing chest surgery, the Met said on Monday. He also remains committed to a run as the title character in a new production of Gounod’s “Faust,” which opens on Nov. 29, and to appearances in the “Ring” cycle in the spring, the Met said. “Jonas Kaufmann has assured the Met through his management that he plans to sing all of his scheduled performances here this season,” according to a company statement. Mr. Kaufmann said on his Web site that he needed to have an operation to remove a node from his chest. “I do not wish anyone to become alarmed reading this, but my physicians have ordered me to have the surgery done as soon as possible, and it will take place after my appearance in Stockholm on Sept. 2,” he said. He is scheduled to sing in the Jussi Björling gala that day at the Royal Opera. Mr. Kaufmann’s Web site lists five other performances in October, starting on Oct. 10.

headline.main: The Tenor Jonas Kaufmann Keeps Plans Despite Surgery

docs.lead_paragraph: American writers eventually come face to face with the barnacle-encrusted myths that we use to invent ourselves: Manifest Destiny, the Greatest Generation — and let’s not forget Honest Abe and plucky little Betsy Ross stitching together the first Stars and Stripes. docs.abstract: How John Frémont’s abolitionist proclamation paved the way to Lincoln’s.
docs.snippet: How John Frémont’s abolitionist proclamation paved the way to Lincoln’s.
docs.lead_paragraph: On Aug. 30, 1861, Maj. Gen. John C. Frémont, commander of the Union Western Department in St. Louis, issued a proclamation of martial law. “All persons who shall be taken with arms in their hands,” he announced, “shall be tried by court-martial, and if found guilty will be shot.” This was harsh, but perhaps to be expected in the strife-torn region. But Frémont went further. “The property, real and personal, of all persons in the State of Missouri, who shall take up arms against the United States, or who shall be directly proven to have taken an active part with their enemies in the field, is declared to be confiscated to their public use, and their slaves, if any they have, are hereby declared freemen.”

headline.main: The First Emancipation Proclamation

docs.snippet: The gender-bending teenage quartet  threw themselves into a heavy, energetic set in the seedy neighborhood of Shinjuku, Tokyo.
docs.lead_paragraph: A little punk, a little glam, and with more than a touch of Gaga and Patricia Fields, Ziyoou-vachi (“Queen Bee”) is not the type of act you’d expect to find on a major record label, but Sony Music Japan snapped up the gender-bending teenage quartet this past year. Celebrating the impending release of their new album at New Japan in the seedy neighborhood of Shinjuku, Tokyo, the band sashayed down a stripper-ish catwalk in the center of the club — not one of them in any less than five-inch heels — and threw themselves into a heavy, energetic set. The drummer and lead singer, Luli-chan and Avu-chan (17 and 19 respectively), are siblings of African-American and Japanese descent. Avu, 6-foot-3 in heels and weighing no more than 110 pounds, is a natural performer. Wearing a dress of her own creation, she captivated the crowd of masked fans with songs sung in Japanese in both “male voice” and “female voice” as she dangled from a spinning handle in the ceiling and coyly hid behind a fan.

headline.main: Notes From the Underground | Ziyoou-vachi

docs.abstract: A SoCal sneaker brand reimagines a classic.
docs.snippet: A SoCal sneaker brand reimagines a classic.
docs.lead_paragraph: Steven Tiller, a co-founder of the retro SoCal sneaker brand SeaVees, was driving to work recently when he heard on NPR that the 50th anniversary of the Peace Corps was coming up. Initiated by an executive order issued by President John F. Kennedy, the Peace Corps Act was passed in 1961, instituting an “army” of volunteers to aid those in developing countries. Sensing an opportunity right in line with SeaVees’s revisionist design philosophy and midcentury aesthetic, Tiller and his business partner, Derek Galkin, began sifting through old photos of Peace Corps volunteers. On their feet? Narrow plimsolls, a common canvas and rubber sneaker for that era. “The idea was to go back in time, reimagine these shoes and hopefully make them cooler,” Tiller said. The resulting slim-lined sneaker in salt-washed canvas has a contrast suede stripe around its rims and a distinct vintage look. docs.lead_paragraph: Kenya’s government has lost its bid to block the prosecution of senior politicians before the International Criminal Court in The Hague. On Tuesday, appeals judges ruled that they had found insufficient evidence that Kenya’s government was investigating the cases, as it had long claimed. The prosecutor has accused six Kenyans, including the deputy prime minister, two former ministers and a former police chief, of orchestrating large-scale violence after the 2007 elections. More than 1,200 people died and several hundred thousand fled their homes. The decision means that the next stage of the criminal proceedings, confirmation of charges, can go ahead in The Hague this week.

headline.main: Kenya: Officials’ Cases to Go Forward

Trivedi, a professor of psychiatry at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, after several of his patients, all suffering from serious depression, mentioned that they felt happier if they went for a walk. docs.abstract: The 15-year-old fashion wunderkind is bringing back the ’90s she never knew.
docs.snippet: The 15-year-old fashion wunderkind is bringing back the ’90s she never knew.
docs.lead_paragraph: When the teenage fashion blogger Tavi Gevinson announced last November that she was joining forces with the editor Jane Pratt to start a magazine modeled after Pratt’s much-mourned Sassy, the blogosphere lit up with excitement. For a generation of women, Sassy — with its indie ethos and straight talk about weighty topics like feminism and sex — was a seminal magazine: it not only changed their expectations of media, but it also changed how they saw themselves. Gevinson seemed the perfect choice to lend the old-media Pratt some new-media fame. Her precocious blog, Style Rookie, has, in a mere three and a half years, made her a darling of the fashion establishment — she has written for Harper’s Bazaar, served as muse for Rodarte’s Target line, sat front row at the Marc Jacobs runway show and been the subject of a profile in The New Yorker. Even so, a few carped that she intended to edit a publication inspired by one that folded in 1996, the year she was born.

headline.main: How Sassy Is Tavi Gevinson?
headline.print_headline: Sassy, Too

Mr. Wilmes is set to start in the coming Broadway transfer of “Chinglish,” the David Henry Hwang comedy about an American businessman who encounters linguistic and cultural difficulties on a trip to China, its press representatives said Wednesday. Jennifer Lim, who played a strong-willed Chinese official in the play’s Chicago production at the Goodman Theater, will reprise her role on Broadway, as will the cast members Angela Lin, Christine Lin, Stephen Pucci, Johnny Wu and Larry Zhang. Leigh Silverman, who directed “Chinglish” in Chicago, will also stay on for the Broadway run, which will be presented at the Longacre Theater. It is scheduled to begin previews Oct. 11 and open Oct. 27.

docs.abstract: A modern sportswear collection of uncommon elegance, from Dior alum Pierre-Henri Mattout.
docs.snippet: A modern sportswear collection of uncommon elegance, from Dior alum Pierre-Henri Mattout.
docs.lead_paragraph: Like Coco Chanel, Pierre-Henri Mattout was born in Saumur, the medieval French town in the Loire Valley famous among wine snobs for its superb cabernet franc appellation, Saumur-Champigny. The town also happens to be an equestrian center of France, home to the Cadre Noir, one of the world’s most prestigious riding schools. “It’s very uptight, very bourgeois and very elegant,” says Mattout, who, as a p’tit garçon, dreamed not of mounting a Lusitano but of being the academy’s head tailor. Accordingly, Mattout’s latest men’s collection — all jodhpur-style chinos, leather elbow patches and whipcord wool blazers in dragoon red — is a paean to his horse-loving hometown. But rather than reboot some bygone vision of aristo chic, Mattout drew on his design experience at Dior Homme, Dunhill and Victorinox. The result is a modern sportswear collection of uncommon elegance, detail-obsessed yet refreshingly remote from the work-wear-inspired stuff that’s glutting American runways.

headline.main: The Cavalier

docs.lead_paragraph: So many thoughts after today’s column, in which I wrote about the Keystone XL pipeline. If it’s approved by President Obama, it would carry diluted bitumen — acidic crude oil — 1,700 miles from the tar sands in Alberta to refineries on the Texas Gulf Coast. The Times has already come out against the pipeline, citing the risk of spills, spikes in greenhouse gas emissions and massive destruction of Canada’s boreal forest. Proponents cite job creation and “oil security.”

headline.main: Keystone XL Is Self-Destructive. Does the Obama Administration Need to Be Also?

docs.abstract: Bucking criticism, federal hurricane forecasters display their skill.
docs.snippet: Bucking criticism, federal hurricane forecasters display their skill.
docs.lead_paragraph: It seems inevitable to have finger-pointing whenever a hurricane makes landfall. If the storm weakens, there are charges of alarmism and fear-mongering. If it veers or strengthens, hammered communities cry out. With Hurricane Irene, it was mostly the former, as various factions with axes to grind piled on the National Hurricane Center. (A case in point was Patrick Michaels, a climate scientist at the anti-regulatory Cato Institute who last Friday said the storm should be renamed “Hurricane Hype,” adding that he doubted it would “cough up even eight bodies.” With the death count far higher, he apologized through the Watts Up With That blog.)
